He said, "The sheets then remained with Abu Bakr until God took him, then with Umar until God took him, then with Hafsa, the daughter of Umar."
Some of the transmitters said that in this report lakhaf means pottery.
He said in Jami al-Usul that al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi transmitted it.

quotes.caption: Uthman, in al-Askari, al-Qur'an al-Karim wa Riwayat al-Madrasatayn, vol.1, p.211

paragraphs.text: في مسند أحمد بسنده عن ابن عباس أنه قال في حديثه عن الخليفة عثمان أنّه قال : إن رسول اللّه ( ص ) كان مما يأتي عليه الزمان ينزل عليه من السور ذوات العدد ، وكان إذا أنزل عليه الشيء يدعو بعض من يكتب عنده ، يقول : ضعوا هذا في السورة التي يذكر فيها كذا وكذا ، وينزل عليه الآيات فيقول : ضعوا هذه الآيات في السورة التي يذكر فيها كذا وكذا ، وينزل عليه الآية فيقول : ضعوا هذه الآية في السورة التي يذكر فيها كذا وكذا (9) .
In the Musnad of Ahmad, with its chain of transmission, from Ibn Abbas, who said in his report about the caliph Uthman that he said.

“Time would often pass for the Messenger of God while a number of surahs were being revealed to him. Whenever something was revealed to him, he would call one of those who wrote for him and say, ‘Put this in the surah in which such and such is mentioned.’ Verses would be revealed to him and he would say, ‘Put these verses in the surah in which such and such is mentioned.’ A verse would be revealed to him and he would say, ‘Put this verse in the surah in which such and such is mentioned.’”

quotes.caption: Imam Ali, Ibn Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Masahif, p.67, no.39

paragraphs.text: [ 39 ] حدثنا (39) عبد اللّه قال حدثنا سهل بن صالح قال قال حدثنا أبو داود ويعقوب قالا أخبرنا شعبة عن علقمة بن مرثد عن سويد بن غفلة قال قال علي في المصاحف لو لم يصنعه عثمان لصنعته [ قال أبو داود « * » عن رجل عن سويد ] .

[39] Abd Allah narrated to us, he said, Sahl ibn Salih narrated to us, he said, he said, Abu Dawud and Yaqub narrated to us, both said, Shuba informed us, from Alqama ibn Marthad, from Suwayd ibn Ghafala, who said.
Ali said about the codices, “If Uthman had not done it, I would have done it.”
[Abu Dawud said, from a man, from Suwayd.]

quotes.caption: al-Saduq, al-I'tiqadat, p.86

paragraphs.text: اعتقادنا أن القرآن الذي أنزله الله تعالى على نبيه محمد ﵌ هو ما بين الدفتين ، وهو ما في أيدي الناس ، ليس بأكثر من ذلك ، ومبلغ سوره عند الناس مائة وأربع عشرة سورة . وعندنا أن الضحى وألم نشرح سورة واحدة ، ولايلاف وألم تر كيف سورة واحدة (1) . ومن نسب إلينا أنا نقول إنه أكثر من ذلك فهو كاذب .

Our belief is that the Quran which God Almighty sent down to His Prophet Muhammad is what lies between the two covers, and it is what is in people's hands. It is not more than that. The number of its surahs among the people is one hundred and fourteen. We hold that al-Duha and Alam Nashrah are one surah, and that Li-Ilaf and Alam Tara Kayfa are one surah. Whoever attributes to us the claim that it is more than that is a liar.

quotes.caption: al-Mufid, al-Masa'il al-Sarawiyya, pp.78-79

paragraphs.text: المسألة التاسعة : صيانة القرآن من التحريف ما قولة - أدام الله تعالى حراسته (1) - في القرآن : أهو ما بين الدفتين ، الذي في أيدي الناس ، أم هل ضاع مما أنزل الله تعالى على نبيه منه شئ ، أم لا ؟ وهل هو ما جمعه أمير المؤمنين ﵇ ، أم ما جمعه عثمان بن عفان على ما يذكره المخالفون ؟ الجواب : لا شك (2) أن الذي بين الدفتين من القرآن جميعه (3) كلام الله تعالى وتنزيله ، وليس فيه شئ من كلام البشر ، وهو جمهور المنزل . والباقي مما أنزله (4) الله تعالى (5) عند المستحفظ للشريعة ، المستودع للأحكام ، لم يضع (1) منه شئ (2) . وإن كان الذي جمع ما بين الدفتين الآن لم يجعله في جملة ما جمع لأسباب (3) دعته إلى ذلك ، منها : قصوره عن معرفة بعضه . ومنها : شكه فيه وعدم تيقنه (4) . ومنها : ما تعمد إخراجه منه . وقد جمع أمير المؤمنين ﵇ القرآن المنزل من أوله إلى آخره ، وألفه بحسب ما وجب من تأليفه ، فقدم المكي على المدني ، والمنسوخ على الناسخ ، ووضع كل شئ منه في محله (5) . فلذلك قاد جعفر بن محمد الصادق ﵉ : " أما والله لو قرئ القرآن كما أنزل لألفيتمونا فيه مسمين كما سمي من كان قبلنا " (6) .

Ninth question, the protection of the Quran from alteration. What is the opinion of the shaykh, may God Almighty prolong his guardianship, about the Quran? Is it what lies between the two covers, which is in people's hands, or has some of what God Almighty sent down to His Prophet been lost, or not? And is it what the Commander of the Faithful collected, or what Uthman ibn Affan collected, as the opponents say?

The answer is that there is no doubt that what lies between the two covers, all of it, is the speech of God Almighty and His revelation, and that nothing in it is the speech of human beings. It is the majority of what was revealed. The rest of what God Almighty revealed is with the one entrusted to preserve the law and to whom the rulings are committed, and none of it has been lost. This is so even though the one who collected what lies between the two covers did not include it all in what he collected, for reasons that led him to that. Among them were his limited knowledge of some of it, his doubt about some of it and his lack of certainty about it, and his deliberate exclusion of some of it.

The Commander of the Faithful collected the revealed Quran from its beginning to its end and arranged it as its arrangement required. He placed the Meccan before the Medinan and the abrogated before the abrogating, and put everything in its proper place. For that reason Jafar ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said, “By God, if the Quran were recited as it was revealed, you would find us named in it, just as those before us were named.”

quotes.caption: al-Mufid, al-Masa'il al-Sarawiyya, p.81

paragraphs.text: غير أن الخبر قد صح عن أئمتنا ﵈ أنهم أمروا بقراءة ما بين الدفتين ، وأن لا (1) يتعداه إلا زيادة فيه ولا نقصان منه حتى يقوم القائم ﵇ فيقرأ للناس (2) القرآن على ما أنزله الله تعالى وجمعه أمير المؤمنين ﵇ (3) .

However, the report has been established as sound from our Imams that they commanded the recitation of what lies between the two covers, and that one should not go beyond it, whether by adding to it or by subtracting from it, until the Riser rises and recites to the people the Quran as God Almighty revealed it and as the Commander of the Faithful collected it.

quotes.caption: al-Mufid, Awa'il al-Maqalat, pp.82-83

paragraphs.text: وأما النقصان فإن العقول لا تحيله ولا تمنع من وقوعه ، وقد امتحنت مقالة من ادعاه ، وكلمت عليه المعتزلة وغيرهم طويلا فلم اظفر منهم بحجة اعتمدها في فساده . وقد قال جماعة من أهل الإمامة إنه لم ينقص من كلمة ولا من آية ولا من سورة ولكن حذف ما كان مثبتا في مصحف أمير المؤمنين ( ع ) من تأويله وتفسير معانيه على حقيقة تنزيله وذلك كان ثابتا منزلا وإن لم يكن من جملة كلام الله تعالى الذي هو القرآن المعجز ، وقد يسمى تأويل القرآن قرآنا قال الله تعالى : ( ولا تعجل بالقرآن من قبل أن يقضى إليك وحيه وقل رب زدني علما ) فسمى تأويل القرآن قرآنا ، وهذا ما ليس فيه بين أهل التفسير اختلاف . وعندي أن هذا القول أشبه من مقال من ادعى نقصان كلم من نفس القرآن على الحقيقة دون التأويل ، وإليه أميل والله أسأل توفيقه للصواب . وأما الزيادة فيه فمقطوع على فسادها من وجه ويجوز صحتها من وجه ، فالوجه الذي أقطع على فساده أن يمكن لأحد من الخلق زيادة مقدار سورة فيه على حد يلتبس به عند أحد من الفصحاء ، وأما الوجه المجوز فهو أن يزاد فيه الكلمة والكلمتان والحرف والحرفان وما أشبه ذلك مما لا يبلغ حد الاعجاز ، ويكون ملتبسا عند أكثر الفصحاء بكلم القرآن ، غير أنه لا بد متى وقع ذلك من أن يدل الله عليه ، ويوضح لعباده عن الحق فيه ، ولست أقطع على كون ذلك بل أميل إلى عدمه وسلامة القرآن عنه ، ومعي بذلك حديث عن الصادق جعفر بن محمد (ع) ، وهذا المذهب بخلاف ما سمعناه عن بني نوبخت - ﵏ - من الزيادة في القرآن والنقصان فيه ، وقد ذهب إليه جماعة من متكلمي الإمامية وأهل الفقه منهم والاعتبار .

As for omission, reason does not rule it out or prevent it from happening. I have examined the claim of those who asserted it, and I have spoken at length about it with the Mu'tazila and others, but I found in them no argument that I could rely on to show it false. A group of the Imamis have said that no word, verse or chapter was left out. What was removed, they say, is what had been written in the codex of the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, namely its interpretation and the explanation of its meanings according to the truth of its revelation. That material was established and sent down, even though it was not part of the speech of God Most High that is the inimitable Quran.

The interpretation of the Quran can also be called Quran. God Most High said, "Do not hasten with the Quran before its revelation is completed to you, and say, 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.'" So He called the interpretation of the Quran "Quran," and the scholars of exegesis do not disagree about this. In my view this position is closer to the truth than the statement of those who claimed that actual words were lost from the Quran itself, rather than from its interpretation. I incline toward it, and I ask God for success in reaching what is correct.

As for addition to the Quran, one kind is certainly false and another kind is possible. The kind I am certain is false is that any human being could add the length of a chapter to it in such a way that it would be confused with the Quran in the judgment of any eloquent speaker. The kind that is possible is that a word or two words, or a letter or two letters, or something similar that does not reach the level of inimitability, was added to it and was mistaken for Quranic words by most eloquent speakers. Even so, if that had happened, God would necessarily have pointed it out and made the truth about it clear to His servants. I am not certain that it happened. I incline instead toward its not having happened and toward the Quran being free of it, and I have a report from al-Sadiq, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, peace be upon him, that supports this.

This position differs from what we heard from the Banu Nawbakht, may God have mercy on them, about addition to the Quran and omission from it. A group of Imami theologians, including their jurists and scholars of reflection, have held to it.

quotes.caption: al-Murtada, al-Dhakhira, pp.361-362

paragraphs.text: فان قيل : كيف يكون أحد الامرين كالآخر والامامية تدّعي تغييرا في القرآن ونقصانا ، وكذلك حشوية أصحاب الحديث ؟ قلنا : قد بيّنا صحة نقل القرآن في المسائل الطرابلسيات (3) ، وأنه غير منقوص ولا مبدّل ولا مغيّر ، وأن العلم بأن هذا القرآن الذي في أيدينا هو الذي ظهر على يد رسول اللّه « ص » كالعلم بالبلدان والحوادث الكبار والوقائع العظام ، والكتب المصنفة المشهورة ، والاشعار المدونة . وذكرنا أن العناية اشتدت بالقرآن والدواعي توفرت على نقله وحراسته وبلغت إلى حدّ لم يبلغه في نقل الحوادث والوقائع والكتب المصنفة ، لأن القرآن معجز النبوة ، وأصل العلم بالشريعة والاحكام الدينية . وكل شيء دعا إلى نقل جميع ما تقدم حاصل فيه ، ويستبدّ بدواع إلى النقل ليست في الحوادث وما أشبهها ، وأن علماء المتكلمين بلغوا في ضبطه وحمايته ، وان عرفوا كل شيء اختلف (1) فيه من اعرابه والقراءات المختلفة في حروفه حتى فرّقوا بين ما روي وعرف ، وبين ما لم يذكر ولم يسطر . فكيف يجوز أن يكون مغيّرا أو منقوصا مع هذه العناية الصادقة والضبط الشديد ؟

If it is asked how one of the two matters can be like the other, when the Imamis claim alteration and diminution in the Quran, and so do the Hashwiyya among the hadith folk, we say that we have already explained the soundness of the transmission of the Quran in al-Masa'il al-Tarabulusiyyat. We showed that it is not diminished, replaced, or altered. We also showed that knowledge that this Quran in our hands is what appeared at the hands of the Messenger of God is like knowledge of countries, great events, major incidents, famous compiled books, and recorded poems.

We mentioned also that care for the Quran was intense, and that the motives to transmit and guard it were abundant, to a degree not reached in the transmission of events, incidents, and compiled books. The reason is that the Quran is the miracle that proves prophethood and the foundation of knowledge of the Law and of religious rulings. Everything that prompted the transmission of all those earlier things is present in it, and it alone has motives for transmission that events and the like do not have. The scholars among the theologians went so far in preserving and protecting it that they even knew everything disputed in it, such as its grammatical inflection and the different readings of its letters, until they distinguished between what was narrated and known and what was not mentioned or written down. So how can it be altered or diminished, given this genuine care and strict preservation?

quotes.caption: al-Tabrisi, Majma' al-Bayan, vol.1, pp.42-43

paragraphs.text: ومن ذلك : الكلام في زيادة القرآن ونقصانه فإنه لا يليق بالتفسير . فأما الزيادة فيه : فمجمع على بطلانه . وأما النقصان منه : فقد روى جماعة من أصحابنا ، وقوم من حشوية العامة ، أن في القرآن تغييرا أو نقصانا ، والصحيح من مذهب أصحابنا خلافه

Of this kind is the discussion of increase and decrease in the Quran, which is unsuitable for exegesis. As for increase in it, its invalidity is unanimously agreed. As for decrease from it, a group of our companions and a group of the Hashwiyya of the general body of Muslims (al-'amma) have narrated that the Quran contains alteration or diminution. The sound position of our companions is the opposite.

quotes.caption: al-Khoei, al-Bayan, p.259

paragraphs.text: ومما ذكرناه : قد تبين للقارئ أن حديث تحريف القرآن حديث خرافة وخيال ، لا يقول به إلا من ضعف عقله ، أو من لم يتأمل في أطرافه حق التأمل ، أو من ألجأه إليه يجب القول به . والحب يعمي ويصم ، وأما العاقل المنصف المتدبر فلا يشك في بطلانه وخرافته .

From what we have mentioned, it has become clear to the reader that the talk of the Qur'an's alteration is a superstitious tale and a fantasy. No one holds it except one whose reason is weak, or one who has not reflected on its aspects with the reflection they deserve, or one whom love of holding the view drives to it. Love blinds and deafens. But the sensible, fair-minded person who reflects has no doubt that it is false and a superstitious tale.

quotes.caption: al-Khomeini, Anwar al-Hidaya, vol.1, pp.207-208

paragraphs.text: أمّا الأولى : فلمنع وقوع التحريف فيه جدّاً ، كما هو مذهب المحقّقين من علماء العامّة والخاصّة ، والمعتبرين من الفريقين ، وإن شئت شطراً من الكلام في هذا المقام فارجع إلى مقدّمة تفسير آلاء الرحمن للعلّامة البلاغي المعاصر ﵋ (2) . وأزيدك توضيحاً : أنّه لو كان الأمر كما توهّم صاحب «فصل الخطاب» الذي كان كتبه لا يفيد علماً ولا عملًا ، وإنّما هو إيراد روايات أعرض عنها الأصحاب ، واختلاط ضعاف بين الروايات بعد تنزيهها عنها أولو الألباب من قدماء أصحابنا كالمحمّدين الثلاثة المتقدّمين ﵏ . هذا حال كتب روايته غالباً ك «المستدرك» ، ولا تسأل عن سائر كتبه المشحونة بالقصص والحكايات الغريبة التي غالبها بالهزل أشبه منه بالجدّ ، وهو ﵀ شخص صالح متتبّع ، إلّاأنّ اشتياقه لجمع الضعاف والغرائب والعجائب وما لا يقبلها العقل السليم والرأي المستقيم ، أكثر من الكلام النافع ، والعجب من معاصريه من أهل اليقظة ! كيف ذهلوا وغفلوا حتّى وقع ما وقع ممّا بكت عليه السماوات ، وكادت تتدكدك على الأرض ؟ ! وبالجملة : لو كان الأمر كما ذكره هذا وأشباهه ، من كون الكتاب الإلهي مشحوناً بذكر أهل البيت وفضلهم ، وذكر أمير المؤمنين وإثبات وصايته وإمامته ، فلِمَ لم يحتجّ بواحد من تلك الآيات النازلة والبراهين القاطعة من الكتاب الإلهي أميرُالمؤمنين ، وفاطمة ، والحسن ، والحسين ﵈ وسلمان ، وأبوذرّ ، ومقداد ، وعمّار ، وسائر الأصحاب الذين لا يزالون يحتجّون على خلافته ﵇ (1) ؟ ! ولمَ تشبّث ﵇ بالأحاديث النبوية (2) ، والقرآن بين أظهرهم ؟ !

As for the first, it is because the occurrence of distortion in it is utterly ruled out, as is the position of the verifying scholars among the general body of Muslims (al-'amma) and the particular group, and of the reliable authorities of both camps. If you want a portion of the discussion on this point, turn to the introduction of the Quran commentary Ala al-Rahman by the great contemporary scholar al-Balaghi. I add a further clarification for you. If the matter were as the author of Fasl al-Khitab imagined, whose books give neither knowledge nor practical benefit, and are only a presentation of reports that the associates turned away from, and a mixing of weak reports among the reports, after people of understanding among our early scholars, such as the three earlier Muhammads, had cleared them of these weak ones.

This is the condition of his books of narration for the most part, such as al-Mustadrak. Do not ask about the rest of his books, which are crammed with strange stories and tales, most of which resemble jest more than earnest. He was a righteous and diligent researcher, except that his eagerness to gather weak, strange and wondrous reports, which sound reason and upright judgment do not accept, was greater than his eagerness for useful discourse. It is astonishing that his contemporaries among the people of alertness were so stunned and heedless that what happened did happen, the thing over which the heavens wept and almost crumbled onto the earth!

In short, if the matter were as he and his like have stated, that the divine Book is crammed with mention of the Ahl al-Bayt and their merit, and with mention of the Commander of the Faithful and proof of his designation as successor and his imamate, then why did none of those revealed verses and decisive proofs from the divine Book get cited as argument by the Commander of the Faithful, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, or by Salman, Abu Dharr, al-Miqdad, Ammar, and the rest of the Companions who kept arguing for his caliphate? And why did he hold fast to the prophetic traditions while the Quran was in their midst?

quotes.caption: al-Sistani, Istifta'at, p.131, no.489

paragraphs.text: 489 . السؤال : لقد قرأت كثيرا في ما ينشر على الانترنت عن موضوع تحريف القرآن ، حيث ينسبونه إلى الشيعة ويستدلون بأدلة من المذهب الشيعي ، فلا أعلم مدى صحة هذه الأقاويل ؟ الجواب : دعوى باطلة أجيب عليها من قبل علماء الشيعة مرات عديدة وهم يكررون القول الباطل وعقيدتنا أن القرآن المنزل من الله تعالى على النبي الأكرم - ﵌ - هو نفس القرآن الموجود لدى المسلمين حاليا من دون زيادة ولا نقيصة .

489. Question. I have read a great deal of what is published on the internet about the subject of the distortion of the Qur'an. They attribute it to the Shia and cite evidence from the Shia school, and I do not know how valid these claims are.

Answer. It is a false claim. Shia scholars have answered it many times, yet they keep repeating the false statement. Our belief is that the Qur'an sent down by God Almighty upon the Noble Prophet is the very Qur'an that Muslims have today, without addition or deficiency.

quotes.caption: al-Fayd al-Kashani, al-Safi, vol.1, p.52

paragraphs.text: أقول : المستفاد من مجمع هذه الأخبار وغيرها من الروايات من طريق أهل البيت (عيهم السلام) إن القرآن الذي بين أظهرنا ليس بتمامه كما انزل على محمد (﵌) منه ما هو خلاف ما أنزل الله ومنه ما هو مغير ومحرف وإنه قد حذف عنه أشياء كثيرة منها اسم علي (﵇) في كثير من المواضع ومنها غير ذلك وأنه ليس أيضا على الترتيب المرضي عند الله وعند رسوله (﵌) .

I say. What is gathered from the whole of these reports and from other narrations by way of the Ahl al-Bayt is that the Qur'an among us is not complete as it was sent down to Muhammad. Part of it is contrary to what God sent down, and part of it is altered and distorted. Many things have been removed from it, among them the name of Ali in many places, and other things besides. It is also not in the order that is pleasing to God and to His Messenger.

quotes.caption: al-Fayd al-Kashani, al-Safi, vol.1, p.54

paragraphs.text: أقول : ويرد على هذا كله إشكال وهو أنه على هذا التقدير لم يبق لنا اعتماد على شئ من القرآن إذ على هذا يحتمل كل آية منه أن يكون محرفا ومغيرا ويكون على خلاف ما أنزل الله فلم يبق لنا في القرآن حجة أصلا فتنتفي فائدته وفائدة الأمر باتباعه والوصية بالتمسك به إلى غير ذلك ، وأيضا قال الله ﷿ : وإنه لكتاب عزيز لا يأتيه الباطل من بين يديه ولا من خلفه . وقال : إنا نحن نزلنا الذكر وإنا له لحافظون فكيف يتطرق إليه التحريف والتغيير ، وأيضا قد استفاض عن النبي (﵌) والأئمة (﵈) حديث عرض الخبر المروي على كتاب الله ليعلم صحته بموافقته له وفساده بمخالفته فإذا كان القرآن الذي بأيدينا محرفا فما فائدة العرض مع أن خبر التحريف مخالف لكتاب الله مكذب له فيجب رده والحكم بفساده أو تأويله .

I say that an objection arises against all of this. On this assumption, we are left with nothing in the Quran that we can rely on. For on this view every verse in it could be altered and changed, and could differ from what God sent down. Then nothing in the Quran would remain a proof for us at all, so its benefit would be lost. The benefit of the command to follow it and of the instruction to hold fast to it would be lost too, and so on.

Also, God, mighty and majestic, said, "And it is indeed a mighty Book. Falsehood cannot come at it from before it or from behind it." And He said, "It is We who sent down the Reminder, and it is We who will guard it." So how could alteration or change reach it?

Also, the hadith about presenting a transmitted report to the Book of God is widely reported from the Prophet and the Imams. By it, the soundness of a report is known through its agreement with the Book, and its falseness through its disagreement. If the Quran in our hands were altered, what would be the use of this presentation? Moreover, the report of alteration contradicts the Book of God and denies it. So it must be rejected and judged false, or else interpreted.

quotes.caption: al-Fayd al-Kashani, al-Safi, vol.1, p.55

paragraphs.text: ولا يبعد أيضا أن يقال إن بعض المحذوفات كان من قبيل التفسير والبيان ولم يكن من أجزاء القرآن فيكون التبديل من حيث المعنى أي حرفوه وغيروه في تفسيره وتأويله أعني حملوه على خلاف ما هو به ، فمعنى قولهم (﵈) كذا نزلت أن المراد به ذلك لا أنها نزلت مع هذه الزيادة في لفظها فحذف منها ذلك اللفظ .

It is also not far-fetched to say that some of the omitted material was explanation and clarification, and was not part of the Quran. In that case the substitution is in the meaning. That is, they altered and changed the Quran in its explanation and interpretation, by which I mean they applied it contrary to what it really means. So the saying of the Imams, "It was revealed thus," means that the intended sense is that one. It does not mean that the verse was revealed with this addition in its wording, and that this wording was then removed from it.

quotes.caption: al-Fayd al-Kashani, al-Safi, vol.1, p.58

paragraphs.text: أقول : يكفي في وجوده في كل عصر وجوده جميعا كما أنزله الله محفوظا عند أهله ووجود ما احتجنا إليه منه عندنا وإن لم نقدر على الباقي كما أن الإمام (﵇) كذلك فان الثقلين سيان في ذلك .

I say, for its existence in every age it is enough that all of it exists, just as God sent it down, preserved with its people, and that what we need of it is with us, even if we are unable to reach the rest. The Imam is the same in this respect, for the two weighty things are alike in that.

blocks.observation: The title "The Preserved Qur'an" states the topic as a settled noun phrase, and the body then supports it by reporting what Imami scholars say, not by asserting it alone.
blocks.text: The Preserved Qur'an

blocks.observation: The summary opens with "Imami scholars from al-Saduq to al-Sistani hold that" the received text is the revealed one, then adds that both schools carry reports, so a reader meets the finding and its limit together.
blocks.text: Imami scholars from al-Saduq to al-Sistani hold that the Qur'an between the two covers is the Qur'an God sent down. Imami books carry reports of loss, and Sunni books carry reports of scribal error. Al-Tusi classed the Imami reports as solitary, and Sunni scholars graded the Sunni reports sound, interpreted them or rejected them. Scholars of both schools disputed what the reports show.

blocks.observation: The page heading "The Preserved Qur'an" repeats the title once for the rendered page and carries no separate claim.
blocks.text: # The Preserved Qur'an

blocks.observation: Premise 1 says "Ibn Hazm charged the Imamiyya" and keeps the charge as his, then gives the exempted man and al-Safadi's quotation, so the identification with al-Murtada is traced to a named biographer.
blocks.text: **Premise 1.** Ibn Hazm charged the Imamiyya with holding that the Qur'an was changed, with words added and many removed. He exempted one Imami and two companions. Al-Safadi quotes the charge in his entry on al-Sharif al-Murtada. His quotation names the exempted man Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa, which is al-Murtada's name.

blocks.observation: Premise 2 fixes the term: tahrif in the Qur'an means "moving words from their places and meanings", and al-Khoei locates the dispute in loss of revealed text, which prevents the later reports being read as one claim.
blocks.text: **Premise 2.** The Qur'an uses tahrif for moving words from their places and meanings. Al-Khoei names the loss of revealed text as the sense of tahrif that Muslims dispute.

blocks.observation: Premise 3 lists what the books carry, using "verses Jibril brought "in this form" with a name added" as a report and not as a verdict, and sets the Sunni Ibn Abbas reports beside the Kafi ones.
blocks.text: **Premise 3.** Al-Kafi carries reports of a larger revelation and of verses Jibril brought "in this form" with a name added. It also carries a report of a scribal error in Qur'an 5:95. Sunni books carry reports in which Ibn Abbas calls words of the codex a scribe's error.

blocks.observation: Premise 4 joins the Imams' two instructions to al-Tusi's grading: "judge reports by the Qur'an" and recite as people recite, with the reports of loss classed as solitary.
blocks.text: **Premise 4.** The Imams ﵈ told their followers to judge reports by the Qur'an. They also told them to recite as the people recite until al-Qa'im rises. Al-Tusi classes the reports of loss as solitary reports, which yield neither certain knowledge nor grounds for action.

blocks.observation: Premise 5 names six scholars who affirm the received text, then names al-Majlisi and al-Fayd al-Kashani as readers of "some reports as evidence of loss", so the division inside the school is stated.
blocks.text: **Premise 5.** Al-Saduq, al-Murtada, al-Khoei, al-Tabataba'i, al-Khomeini and al-Sistani hold that the Qur'an in Muslim hands is the Qur'an God sent down. Al-Tabrisi calls that the sound view of the school, and al-Tusi calls it the view more fitting for the sound position of his school. Al-Majlisi, and al-Fayd al-Kashani in al-Safi, read some reports as evidence of loss.

blocks.observation: The conclusion draws a limited result: "some Imami scholars accepted reports of omission" while the named scholars affirm the received Qur'an, and Ibn Hazm's charge turns that dispute into doctrine.
blocks.text: **Conclusion.** Imami scholars including al-Saduq, al-Murtada, al-Khoei, al-Tabataba'i, al-Khomeini and al-Sistani affirm the received Qur'an, and some Imami scholars accepted reports of omission. Sunni books carry reports of scribal error, which Sunni scholars accepted, interpreted or rejected. Al-Tusi classed the Imami reports of loss as solitary, and scholars of both schools disputed what the reports show. Ibn Hazm's charge presents that dispute as the doctrine of the Imamiyya.

blocks.observation: The heading "The Charge Ibn Hazm Recorded" says the section reports a charge, so the title does not assert that the charge is true.
blocks.text: ## The Charge Ibn Hazm Recorded

blocks.observation: The source line "Ibn Hazm, al-Fisal fi al-Milal wa al-Ahwa' wa al-Nihal, vol.4, p.182" gives the full title, volume and page, and adds al-Safadi's volume and pages.
blocks.text: - **Source:** Ibn Hazm, al-Fisal fi al-Milal wa al-Ahwa' wa al-Nihal, vol.4, p.182; al-Safadi, al-Wafi bil-Wafayat, vol.21, pp.2-3

blocks.observation: The speaker line "Ibn Hazm al-Andalusi (d.456 AH); Salah al-Din al-Safadi (d.764 AH)" dates both men, which shows the charge reaches the reader through a later biographer.
blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Ibn Hazm al-Andalusi (d.456 AH); Salah al-Din al-Safadi (d.764 AH)

blocks.observation: The claim line "all Imamiyya hold the Qur'an was altered, except one named Imami" reports the charge in indirect speech and keeps the exemption inside it.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** all Imamiyya hold the Qur'an was altered, except one named Imami and his two companions

blocks.observation: The paragraph explains the passage in ordinary words, for example "surveys religions and sects in al-Fisal", and reports the printed name of the exempted man and his two companions before any comparison.
blocks.text: Ibn Hazm, an Andalusian scholar, surveys religions and sects in al-Fisal. He attributes the view of an altered Qur'an to all the Imamiyya, the Imami Shia, early and late. He exempts one Imami with Mu'tazili leanings. The printed al-Fisal names him Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Musa and traces his descent to Musa ibn Ja'far. Ibn Hazm reports that this man rejected the view and called its holders unbelievers. He reports the same of two companions, Abu Ya'la Milad al-Tusi and Abu al-Qasim al-Razi.

blocks.observation: The paragraph compares two lineages and concludes "rests on al-Safadi's quotation of Ibn Hazm", which limits the identification to what the two texts show.
blocks.text: Al-Safadi, a biographer of the eighth century AH, quotes this passage in his entry on al-Sharif al-Murtada. The entry opens with al-Murtada's lineage, Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Musa, traced to Musa ibn Ja'far. In the quotation, Ibn Hazm exempts a man of that same name, so al-Safadi treats the exempted man as al-Murtada. The printed al-Fisal gives the lineage in a different form. It has al-Hasan where al-Safadi has al-Husayn, at the start and near the end of the chain. It also lacks one Musa between Muhammad and Ibrahim. The identification of the exempted man with al-Murtada therefore rests on al-Safadi's quotation of Ibn Hazm.

blocks.observation: The heading "What Tahrif Means" names the term the section fixes before any report is read.
blocks.text: ## What Tahrif Means

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Jawhari, al-Sihah, vol.4, p.31" cites the first lexicon with volume and page, and Ibn Manzur's Lisan al-Arab with its volume and page.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Jawhari, al-Sihah, vol.4, p.31; Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab, vol.9, p.43

blocks.observation: The speaker line "Speaker: two classical lexicographers" identifies the voices by profession and leaves their dates to the table.
blocks.text: - **Speaker:** two classical lexicographers

blocks.observation: The claim line "tahrif of speech is changing it" states the lexical result and adds that the Qur'an uses the verb for changing meanings.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** tahrif of speech is changing it, and the Qur'an uses the verb for changing meanings

blocks.observation: The paragraph gives both definitions and ties Ibn Manzur's quoted words "they distort words from their places" to Qur'an 4:46 and 5:13.
blocks.text: Al-Jawhari defines the tahrif of speech as changing it from its places. Ibn Manzur says the Jews changed the meanings of the Torah by look-alikes. He quotes the Qur'an's words "they distort words from their places", which occur in Qur'an 4:46 and 5:13.

blocks.observation: The verse line "Verse: Qur'an 4:46" locates the verse quoted in the callout beneath it.
blocks.text: - **Verse:** Qur'an 4:46

blocks.observation: The claim line "some of the Jews distort words from their places" renders the verse in plain words for the reader of the Arabic callout.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** some of the Jews distort words from their places

blocks.observation: The paragraph counts the verb's four uses and concludes "None of the four verses applies the verb to the Qur'an", a fact about the verses and not a verdict on later reports.
blocks.text: The Qur'an uses the verb four times, in Qur'an 2:75, 4:46, 5:13 and 5:41. Each verse describes people who alter the sense or the place of words in an earlier scripture. None of the four verses applies the verb to the Qur'an.

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Khoei, al-Bayan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, pp.197 and 200" names the work and the two pages quoted.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Khoei, al-Bayan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, pp.197 and 200

blocks.observation: The speaker line "Sayyid Abu al-Qasim al-Khoei (d.1413 AH)" names and dates the scholar whose classification follows.
blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Sayyid Abu al-Qasim al-Khoei (d.1413 AH)

blocks.observation: The claim line "tahrif has several senses, and loss of text is the one in dispute" states his classification before the passages are quoted.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** tahrif has several senses, and loss of text is the one in dispute among Muslims

blocks.observation: The paragraph walks through the senses in order and discloses that "The passages quoted here leave out his second to fourth senses", then draws the practical rule that a report of loss must speak of lost text.
blocks.text: Al-Khoei sorts the senses of tahrif by whether Muslims agree they occurred. His first sense is moving a thing from its place, and he applies it to interpreting a verse against its meaning. He says all Muslims agree that this kind of tahrif occurred. His fifth sense is addition of material that is not revealed speech, which he calls false by consensus. His sixth sense is omission, and he names it as the sense in dispute. The passages quoted here leave out his second to fourth senses. A report that uses the word tahrif may therefore mean a false interpretation. To support a charge of loss, a report has to speak of lost text.

blocks.observation: The paragraph qualifies the consensus on addition by naming two positions, "Al-Mufid allows that a word or a letter could be added", and al-Mazandarani's copyist reading, so al-Khoei's claim does not stand unqualified.
blocks.text: Two positions below conflict with al-Khoei's claim of consensus on addition. Al-Mufid allows that a word or a letter could be added to the Qur'an. Al-Mazandarani reads the report on Qur'an 5:95 as a copyist's added letter.

blocks.observation: The heading "The Guarantee of Qur'an 15:9" names the verse and the guarantee al-Tabataba'i reads from it.
blocks.text: ## The Guarantee of Qur'an 15:9

blocks.observation: The verse line "Verse: Qur'an 15:9" locates the verse in the callout.
blocks.text: - **Verse:** Qur'an 15:9

blocks.observation: The claim line "God sent down the Reminder and guards it" renders the verse in plain words.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** God sent down the Reminder and guards it

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, vol.12, p.107" cites the commentary with volume and page.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, vol.12, p.107

blocks.observation: The speaker line "Allama Muhammad Husayn al-Tabataba'i (d.1402 AH)" names and dates the commentator.
blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Allama Muhammad Husayn al-Tabataba'i (d.1402 AH)

blocks.observation: The claim line "the Qur'an in hand carries every attribute God gave it" gives his argument in one sentence before the quotation.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** the Qur'an in hand carries every attribute God gave it, so it is the Qur'an sent down

blocks.observation: The paragraph explains the argument step by step, from attributes to traces to the conclusion, and keeps his own limit: "A dropped repeated verse, or a difference in a dot or a vowel, would leave the attributes intact."
blocks.text: Al-Tabataba'i reasons from the Qur'an's attributes to its text. God described the Qur'an as inimitable, free of discrepancy, guiding and luminous. If addition, omission or a change of wording or order had altered those attributes, their traces would show the change. The Qur'an in hand carries those traces in full, so he concludes it is the Qur'an sent down. A dropped repeated verse, or a difference in a dot or a vowel, would leave the attributes intact. He says any loss, if one supposes it, would have to be of that kind.

blocks.text: ## Reports in al-Kafi

blocks.observation: The claim line "this report and many sound reports state loss" gives al-Majlisi's claim, with mutawatir named as its strength.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** this report and many sound reports state loss, and their meaning is mutawatir

blocks.observation: The paragraph defines both terms where they occur, "Mutawatir means reported by so many routes that the shared meaning is certain", and reports his comparison with the reports on the imamate.
blocks.text: Al-Milani quotes al-Majlisi's comment on a report that al-Majlisi graded muwaththaq, reliable through trustworthy narrators who include non-Imamis. Al-Majlisi then calls the reports of loss mutawatir in meaning. Mutawatir means reported by so many routes that the shared meaning is certain. He judges them at least equal to the reports on the imamate.

blocks.observation: The paragraph reports al-Milani's reply in his name, including that most Kafi reports of loss are graded "graded most of the al-Kafi reports of loss weak or mursal", and defines mursal in the next sentence.
blocks.text: Al-Milani answers that al-Majlisi's Bihar al-Anwar calls such reports solitary. He cites al-Murtada, al-Tusi, al-Fayd and al-Saduq against the claim of soundness. He adds that al-Majlisi graded most of the al-Kafi reports of loss weak or mursal. A mursal report has a gap in its chain. Al-Milani asks whether that equality refers to number, strength of meaning or soundness of chains.

blocks.text: - **Claim:** a man is told to stop a non-standard reading and to recite as the people recite until al-Qa'im rises

blocks.observation: The paragraph retells the report in order and ends on a limit the source allows: "it does not say how the two differed".
blocks.text: Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ stops the man's reading and tells him to recite as the people recite. The instruction holds until al-Qa'im, the Riser from the Prophet's ﷺ house, rises. The Imam ﵇ says al-Qa'im will bring out the codex Ali ﵇ wrote. He recounts that Ali ﵇ offered that codex as the Book sent down to Muhammad ﷺ. The people answered that their own codex held the whole Qur'an. The report sets Ali's ﵇ codex apart from the circulating copy, and it does not say how the two differed.

blocks.text: - **Claim:** whoever claims to have gathered the whole Qur'an as it was revealed is a liar, except Ali ﵇ and the Imams after him

blocks.text: The chapter heading says that only the Imams gathered the whole Qur'an and that "they know all of its knowledge". Jabir's report says Ali ﵇ and the Imams after him gathered and memorized it "as God Most High sent it down". The report gives no account of what the people's copy lacked.

blocks.text: Reports of this form add a name to a verse and say Jibril brought the verse "in this form". Al-Kulayni gathered them in a chapter on wilaya, the authority of the Imams. Al-Tabataba'i reads such wording as the explanation that accompanied the revelation, as quoted below.

blocks.observation: The claim line "many such reports have weak chains" includes the qualifier that some come by reliable routes, so the claim is not stated one-sidedly.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** many such reports have weak chains, a large share come from al-Sayyari, and some come by reliable routes

blocks.observation: The paragraph reports al-Khoei's criticism, al-Najashi's grade of al-Sayyari and the count "350 of the 1,602 reports", then al-Khoei's concession that some reports certainly came from the Imams.
blocks.text: Al-Khoei says many reports of tahrif have weak chains. He traces a number of them to the book of Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari and others to Ali ibn Ahmad al-Kufi. Al-Najashi calls al-Sayyari weak in hadith and corrupt in doctrine, with many mursal reports. Al-Muhammadi counts 350 of the 1,602 reports gathered by the hadith scholar al-Nuri as coming from al-Sayyari's Book of Recitations. Al-Khoei grants that the number of reports makes it certain that some came from the Imams ﵈. He holds that none of them indicates tahrif in the disputed sense, the loss of text.

blocks.text: ## How the School Weighs a Solitary Report

blocks.observation: The claim line "reports of loss are solitary" states al-Tusi's classification and his advice to set the reports aside.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** reports of loss are solitary, yield neither knowledge nor grounds for action, and are best set aside

blocks.observation: The paragraph paraphrases al-Tusi in the order of his passage, from consensus on addition to his remark that even a sound report "would not challenge the text between the covers".
blocks.text: Al-Tusi calls addition invalid by consensus. He calls the denial of loss the apparent position of Muslims and the view more fitting for the sound position of his school. He grants that narrators of his school and of the general body of Muslims transmit many reports of loss and of moved verses. He classes them as solitary reports, which yield neither certain knowledge nor grounds for action. He adds that even a sound report of this kind would not challenge the text between the covers.

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Kafi, vol.1, p.69, no.5; al-Hurr al-Amili, Wasa'il al-Shi'a" cites two reports for the rule that the Book tests reports.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Kafi, vol.1, p.69, no.5; al-Hurr al-Amili, Wasa'il al-Shi'a, vol.27, p.118, no.33362

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, quoting the Prophet ﷺ; and Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, through Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abd Allah

blocks.observation: The claim line "a report that contradicts the Book of God is rejected" states the rule both reports teach.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** a report that contradicts the Book of God is rejected

blocks.observation: The paragraph applies the rule: "A report that the Book was altered contradicts that Book, so it fails the test." The application is the school's inference, and the next sentence attributes it to al-Fayd.
blocks.text: The Mina sermon makes the Book the test for any report from the Prophet ﷺ. The Wasa'il report makes it the test between two differing hadiths. A report that the Book was altered contradicts that Book, so it fails the test. Al-Fayd al-Kashani applies this rule to the reports of alteration in al-Safi, quoted in the section on the scholars of the school.

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Kafi, vol.2, pp.630-631, nos.12, 13 and 15" cites three reports by number.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Kafi, vol.2, pp.630-631, nos.12, 13 and 15

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Imam al-Baqir ﵇ and Imam al-Sadiq ﵇

blocks.observation: The claim line "the Qur'an is one, sent down by One" states what the three reports teach, with recitation as taught.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** the Qur'an is one, sent down by One, and differences come from the narrators; recite as you were taught

blocks.observation: The paragraph summarizes the three reports in order, glosses ahruf as "modes of reading", and quotes the answer "Recite as you were taught" without adding a conclusion.
blocks.text: Imam al-Baqir ﵇ says the Qur'an is one and the disagreement comes from the transmitters. Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ denies that the Qur'an came down in seven ahruf, modes of reading, and says it came down in one. Asked about the Qur'an's revelation, he answers, "Recite as you were taught."

blocks.text: - **Source:** Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, al-Musnad, vol.8, p.470, no.5057

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ

blocks.observation: The claim line "two men taught different readings are told to recite as they were taught" states the report's content.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** two men taught different readings are told to recite as they were taught

blocks.observation: The sentence "Sunni books report the same words from the Prophet" introduces the parallel and states that the words are the same.
blocks.text: Sunni books report the same words from the Prophet ﷺ.

blocks.observation: The paragraph compares the two reports and concludes that the Prophet's instruction "leaves two readings in place" while the Imam's names one, a difference taken directly from their wording.
blocks.text: In Ibn Mas'ud's report, two men each say the Prophet ﷺ taught them a sura. The Prophet ﷺ tells both to recite as they were taught. Each man keeps the reading he was taught. In Salim's report, the Imam ﵇ tells the man to recite as the people recite until al-Qa'im rises. The Prophet's ﷺ instruction leaves two readings in place, and the Imam's ﵇ instruction names one, the people's reading.

blocks.observation: The source line "al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, vol.12, p.108" continues the commentary on the next page.
blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, vol.12, p.108

blocks.observation: The speaker line "Speaker: al-Tabataba'i" names the commentator with no date, since the date appears earlier.
blocks.text: - **Speaker:** al-Tabataba'i

blocks.observation: The claim line "the Imams argued from the Qur'an as it stands" gives his claim and its gloss of "it was revealed thus" as explanation.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** the Imams ﵈ argued from the Qur'an as it stands, and "it was revealed thus" means explanation

blocks.observation: The paragraph separates his three groups of reports and ends on his own limit: any difference lies "only in the order of the suras or of some verses".
blocks.text: Al-Tabataba'i draws on three groups of reports. In the first, the Imams ﵈ cite verses on every subject in agreement with the Qur'an in hand. He takes this to show that "it was revealed thus" in many reports means the explanation that came with revelation. In the second, the Imams ﵈ call the people's Qur'an revealed by God, although it differs from Ali's ﵇ codex. The third is their instruction to recite as the people recite. He concludes that any difference from Ali's ﵇ codex lies only in the order of the suras or of some verses, whose reordering leaves the meaning unchanged.

blocks.text: ## Hammad's Report on Qur'an 5:95

blocks.text: - **Verse:** Qur'an 5:95

blocks.text: - **Claim:** two just men among you judge the equivalent of game killed in the state of ihram

blocks.text: - **Source:** al-Kafi, vol.8, p.205, no.247, in al-Rawda

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, through Hammad ibn Uthman

blocks.observation: The claim line "the dual dhawa 'adl, "two just men", is "among the things in which the kuttab erred"" quotes the report's key words and gives the singular reading.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** the dual dhawa 'adl, "two just men", is "among the things in which the kuttab erred", and the reading is dhu 'adl, "one just man"

blocks.observation: The paragraph reduces the report to "The report concerns one letter, the alif", which tells the reader how small the alleged error is.
blocks.text: Hammad recites the dual, and the Imam ﵇ answers with the singular and attributes the dual to the kuttab. The report concerns one letter, the alif that makes "one just man" into "two just men".

blocks.observation: The paragraph reports that "Al-Tabrisi records the singular as the reading of al-Baqir" and al-Sadiq, and classes it among the shawadhdh, defined in the same sentence.
blocks.text: Al-Tabrisi records the singular as the reading of al-Baqir ﵇ and al-Sadiq ﵇. He lists it among the shawadhdh, readings reported outside the accepted readings.

blocks.observation: The paragraph sets two reports side by side and concludes "Al-Tabrisi and Zurara therefore differ on what", a conclusion read directly from their wording.
blocks.text: In Zurara's report Imam al-Baqir ﵇ recites the dual. He names the two just men as the Messenger ﷺ and the Imam after him. Al-Tabrisi and Zurara therefore differ on what al-Baqir ﵇ recited.

blocks.observation: The paragraph lists how five scholars read the kuttab's error, from al-Mazandarani to al-Gulpaygani, and ends on the plain conditional "On the copyist reading, the report alleges a scribal error in the codex".
blocks.text: On the common reading that al-Mazandarani reports, the kuttab erred by giving "two just men" a general application. Al-Mazandarani prefers a second reading, in which the kuttab were copyists and the revealed word was singular. Al-Tabataba'i also takes the kuttab to be the scribes of the codex. Al-Fayd suggests that the one just man is the infallible Imam. Al-Gulpaygani first reads the alif as a scribe's addition. He then judges the dual correct on the strength of Zurara's report. On the copyist reading, the report alleges a scribal error in the codex.

blocks.text: - **Claim:** "the likeness of His light" in Qur'an 24:35 is a scribe's error for "the light of the believer"

blocks.observation: The paragraph records how Sunni and Imami scholars received these reports: Abu Hayyan's harsh judgment, Ibn Ashtah's ahruf explanation and Ma'rifat's review of "reviews ten such reports of early scribal error".
blocks.text: Abu Shahba quotes the exegete Abu Hayyan, who calls whoever reports the 24:27 statement from Ibn Abbas a heretic. Ibn Ashtah, quoted by al-Suyuti, explains the error as a poor choice among the seven ahruf. Ma'rifat, an Imami scholar, reviews ten such reports of early scribal error. He says they must be interpreted or rejected.

blocks.text: Al-Hakim graded the 24:27 report sahih by the standard of al-Bukhari and Muslim.

blocks.text: The Kafi reports speak of a Mushaf of Fatimah ﵍. The word mushaf means any bound collection of pages, as the two sources below define it.

blocks.text: Al-Layth defines the mushaf as written sheets gathered between two covers. Al-Askari concludes that the word names any bound book, Qur'an or not.

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, through Abu Basir, Hammad ibn Uthman and al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Ala'

blocks.observation: The claim line "holds no letter of the Qur'an" states the Imam's own words.
blocks.text: - **Claim:** the Mushaf of Fatimah ﵍ holds no letter of the Qur'an

blocks.observation: The paragraph describes the three reports in order and ends on the Imam's own words, "I do not claim that it contains a Qur'an", which are quoted and not paraphrased.
blocks.text: In the first report Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ says the book is three times the size of the Qur'an. He swears it holds no letter of the Qur'an. In the second, an angel consoles Fatimah ﵍ after the Prophet's ﷺ death, and Ali ﵇ writes down what she hears. The Imam ﵇ says the book holds no law and holds knowledge of what will happen. In the third, he lists the Mushaf of Fatimah ﵍ among the contents of the White Jafr. He adds, "I do not claim that it contains a Qur'an."

blocks.text: Imam Ali ﵇ says the Prophet ﷺ dictated every revealed verse to him and he wrote it in his own hand. He says the Prophet ﷺ also taught him each verse's interpretation, its abrogating and abrogated verses, and its decisive and ambiguous verses. He adds that the Prophet ﷺ prayed for his memory and that he forgot nothing.

blocks.text: Imam Ali ﵇ says he gathered the Qur'an after burying the Prophet ﷺ and the people refused it. The report of Salim ibn Salama gives the same refusal. Neither report says how Ali's ﵇ copy differed. Al-Mufid inclines to the view that the removed material was Ali's ﵇ interpretation. Al-Tabataba'i places any difference in the order of suras or of some verses.

blocks.text: - **Speaker:** Imam Ali ﵇, without an isnad

blocks.text: Sermon 176 calls "this Qur'an" an adviser who does not deceive and a guide who does not lead astray. Sermon 156 tells its hearers to hold fast to the Book of God as the firm rope. Nahj al-Balagha gives both sermons without a chain of transmission.

blocks.text: Radiocarbon analysis dated the parchment of the two Birmingham leaves to between 568 and 645 CE, with 95.4 per cent accuracy. Each manuscript uses the same one of two possible spellings at the same places. He argues that only a single written archetype explains this agreement. On his argument, a project to codify the text took place in the first Islamic century. Sadeghi and Bergmann describe a manuscript from the first half of the seventh century CE. Its text does not belong to the Uthmanic tradition. They report it as the only known manuscript of that kind. These studies support an early written standard text. They do not show what the Companions' earlier copies contained.

Al-Mufid calls their view closer to the truth and inclines toward it. He rules out the addition of a sura's length, and he allows that a word or a letter could be added. blocks.text: Al-Fayd reads the reports as showing that the Qur'an in hand is incomplete, partly altered and out of order. He counts Ali's ﵇ name among the things removed. He lists three objections to that reading. No verse could be relied on, and Qur'an 15:9 and 41:42 would be contradicted. Qur'an 41:42 says falsehood cannot reach the Book. The rule of judging reports by the Book would also lose its use. He allows that some omitted material was explanation, so that "it was revealed thus" gives the intended sense. He concludes that the whole Qur'an exists, preserved with "its people" (ahlihi), a phrase for which he names no group. The part the community needs is in its hands, even if it cannot reach the rest. He likens the Qur'an to the Imam, who also exists beyond the community's reach. Al-Mufid's Sarawiyya places the rest of the revelation with the guardian of the law, which resembles this answer.

# Advisor report: prose

Scope. I read every authored sentence: title, summary, abstract (Premises 1-5 and Conclusion), the Facts table, section lead-ins, card text, body paragraphs, glossary and Final Verdict. I treated everything inside the `[!note]`, `[!tip]`, `[!quote]`, `[!info]`, `[!warning]` callouts as source text or accepted translation and did not review it for style. The scanner reports 0 cues; I read every sentence regardless. The file has no em dashes. Findings below are the defects I could locate; passages I judged clean are listed at the end with reasons.

Finding IDs are P-01 to P-31. Where I say "preserve", the named meaning must survive the edit.

## A. Opening matter (title, summary, abstract)

**P-01. Summary.**
Sentence: "The leading Imami scholars hold that the Qur'an between the two covers is the whole revealed Qur'an, and they treat the reports of loss in their books the way Sunni scholars treat Ibn Abbas's reports of scribal error in theirs."
Defect: two inferences in one 40-word sentence; analogy ("the way") carries a comparison the evidence only partly supports (see P-24). "Leading" is undefined and recurs as "dominant" in the Conclusion and "chief" in P-04.
Contributes: the answer plus the parallel-reports argument.
Action: rewrite. Preserve: (1) the named scholars hold the Qur'an in hand to be complete; (2) Imami books carry reports of loss and Sunni books carry reports of scribal error, and both schools classed such reports as unreliable. Split into two sentences and use one term ("the leading scholars", with the list in Premise 5 as the referent) throughout.

**P-02. Abstract, Conclusion.**
Sentence: "The reports document a dispute over solitary narrations within both schools, and the charge treats that dispute as the doctrine of one school."
Defect: abstract noun stack ("a dispute over solitary narrations"); personification ("the charge treats"); vague. Ibn Hazm's accusation is the actor, not "the charge". "Document" overstates what the reports do.
Contributes: the scope-shift finding (a transmitter-level dispute presented as school doctrine).
Action: rewrite. Preserve: Imami and Sunni books both contain reports that suggest loss or scribal error; scholars of each school disputed their reliability; Ibn Hazm attributed to the whole Imamiyya what some Imami transmitters and a minority of scholars held.

**P-03. Abstract, Conclusion.**
Sentence: "A minority of Imami scholars dissented, and Sunni scholars faced parallel reports in their own books."
Defect: "faced" is mild personification; "in their own books" is source-as-performance (the "own" adds no fact). "Minority" is used for scholars the article elsewhere says include al-Mufid's allowance (see P-30).
Action: rewrite. Preserve: some Imami scholars (name al-Fayd and al-Majlisi) read the reports as evidence of loss; Sunni books contain reports of the same kind.

## B. Ibn Hazm section

**P-04. "The Charge Ibn Hazm Recorded", closing paragraph.**
Sentences: "His exception then names the leading Imami theologian of his own century." "Al-Murtada denied the claim and judged its holders unbelievers, by Ibn Hazm's own report." "The charge therefore described some Imami transmitters, and its author knew that the school's chief scholar rejected it."
Defects: (a) "then names" narrates the order of the source's clauses; (b) "leading ... of his own century" and "chief scholar" are unsupported superlatives, and the two differ; (c) "by Ibn Hazm's own report" is the boasting-from-the-opponent's-own-source pattern the contract bans; (d) "described some Imami transmitters" is an unexplained claim (no evidence in the article shows which transmitters), and "its author knew" attributes knowledge and implies bad faith that the quoted text does not establish; Ibn Hazm shows he knew al-Murtada's denial, not what he thought of its weight.
Contributes: the point that Ibn Hazm's own text exempts al-Murtada and two companions.
Action: rewrite to two sentences. Preserve: Ibn Hazm attributes the view to every Imami, early and late; he exempts Ali ibn al-Hasan (al-Murtada) and two companions, who rejected the view and called its holders unbelievers; so his universal claim is contradicted within his own sentence. Delete "then names", "by Ibn Hazm's own report", "chief scholar", and the transmitters clause unless a located source for it is added.

## C. What Tahrif Means

**P-05.** Sentences: "Al-Jawhari defines the word as changing speech from its places. Ibn Manzur adds that the Jews changed the meanings of the Torah by its near likenesses. He cites the Qur'anic phrase that describes them."
Defect: restates the two callouts directly above; the third sentence repeats the quotation inside the Ibn Manzur callout. Source narration.
Contributes: the lexical definition and the link to the Qur'anic usage.
Action: delete the third sentence; compress the first two into one that states the lexical point: the lexicons define tahrif as changing words from their places, and Ibn Manzur applies it to the Jews' changing of the Torah's meanings by look-alike words. Preserve the Jawhari/Ibn Manzur attribution.

**P-06.** Sentence: "A report that speaks of tahrif may therefore mean a false interpretation. A charge of tahrif has to show that the report means lost text."
Defect: "A charge of tahrif" is an abstract subject; "has to show" shifts burden without naming who. Inference is useful.
Action: rewrite. Preserve: the word tahrif in a report can denote misinterpretation; a critic who cites such a report as evidence of loss must show the report refers to lost text.

## D. The Guarantee of Qur'an 15:9

**P-07.** Sentences: "The argument runs from effect to text." "Al-Tabataba'i states a limit."
Defect: both announce what the next sentence does. The second announces a limit and then states it in the following sentence.
Action: delete both; begin "God described the Qur'an as ..." and begin the limit with "A dropped repeated verse or a difference in a dot or a vowel would leave those attributes intact, so his proof does not exclude it."

**P-08.** Sentence: "A change in wording or order would remove those effects."
Defect (prose and source-review): the source says a change "that affects" the attribute would affect it. The article's sentence states the stronger universal claim, then the next paragraph's limit contradicts it. Also the Facts-table row ("The Qur'an keeps every attribute God gave it, so no loss touches its substance") strengthens the source in the same way.
Action: rewrite. Preserve the conditional: a change that affected the Qur'an's inimitability, guidance or freedom from contradiction would show in those traits. Fix the table row to match.

## E. Reports in al-Kafi

# Economy review (role: economy)

Locators are line numbers in the hashed candidate. I read all 836 lines, the contract, the drafting guide, the council profile and the debate-mode reference. I judged authored prose only: premise cards, Claim bullets, paragraphs after callouts, glossary and verdict. Source text inside callouts is untouched, except where I name a callout as a candidate for removal because it repeats another callout. Deletions come first in each finding. A replacement is given only where a fact or inference would otherwise be lost.

The dominant defect is one pattern, repeated about twenty times: a callout with a clear English translation is followed by a paragraph that re-narrates it sentence by sentence ("X says A. He adds B. He then cites C."), and sometimes a last sentence restates the article's thesis. The second pattern is the thesis itself (minority position, Sunni parallel, solitary reports) stated in the summary line, the abstract Conclusion, the Majlisi paragraph, the Fayd paragraph and the Final Verdict.
