Sentence: "The charge therefore described some Imami transmitters, and its author knew that the school's chief scholar rejected it."
Defect: "some Imami transmitters" appears for the first time here, with no source; the reader cannot tell who they are or how the article knows. "knew" attributes a mental state the quotation does not show. The paragraph also never links the lineage in the quotation ("Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Musa ... ibn Abi Talib") to al-Sharif al-Murtada; the reader sees a list of ancestors and must trust the sentence before it. The Arabic and translation read "al-Hasan" where al-Murtada is Ali ibn al-Husayn; the identification needs a source check.
Action: rewrite. Say what Ibn Hazm's exception shows: he names an Imami who rejected the view and called its holders unbelievers, so "all Imamis, early and late" is Ibn Hazm's overstatement by his own report. Delete "knew". Add the one clause that identifies the lineage as al-Murtada. Source-review the Hasan/Husayn reading.

**R-16. Lines 83, 95 (What Tahrif Means).**
Sentence: "Ibn Manzur adds that the Jews changed the meanings of the Torah by its near likenesses."
Defect: "near likenesses" (translation "look-alikes") has no example, so the reader cannot picture the mechanism. It does not carry the later argument either.
Action: delete, or rewrite with the concrete meaning of the Arabic (source-review). Preserve that Ibn Manzur ties tahrif in the Qur'an to the Jews' handling of the Torah.

**R-17. Line 95-115 (the six senses).**
Sentence: "The first sense is misreading the meaning, and al-Khoei says every Muslim agrees it happened. The fifth sense is addition to the text, ... The sixth sense is loss, and only this sense is in dispute."
Defect: the reader is told there are six senses and shown three. Senses two to four, which the quotation at p.197 groups into "occurs", "does not occur" and "disputed", are never named. "Misreading" is also looser than Khoei's "moving a thing from its place and turning it into something else". The bullet says "Muslims dispute only one of them", which the reader cannot check against the three-way division in the quotation.
Action: rewrite. State in one clause what senses two to four cover and why they are not disputed, or say that the article does not quote them (source-review p.197-200). Preserve Khoei's claim that only omission is disputed.

**R-18. Line 142 (15:9 argument).**
Sentences: "A change in wording or order would remove those effects. ... A dropped repeated verse or a difference in a dot or a vowel would leave those attributes intact, so his proof does not exclude it."
Defect: the two sentences contradict as written. The first says any change in wording or order removes the effects; the second says some changes leave them intact. The quotation says only a change that affects the attribute would. "it" in the last clause has no singular antecedent (a verse, a dot, a vowel).
Action: rewrite. "A change that damaged inimitability, consistency or guidance would show in the Qur'an we have. It shows none. Al-Tabataba'i allows that a dropped repeated verse or a difference in a dot or vowel would leave those attributes intact, so his argument does not exclude such changes." This preserves his stated limit.

**R-19. Line 151 (Kafi, 17,000 verses).**
Sentence: "The Qur'an in hand has a little over six thousand verses, so this report is the one most often cited for loss."
Defect: "so" presents the verse count as the reason for the report's citation frequency. The reader gets no source for "most often cited" and no figure for the count. Whom the report is cited by (Sunni polemicists, al-Nuri) is left out.
Action: rewrite or source-review. Name who cites it, or delete the claim of frequency. Preserve the verse-count comparison.

**R-20. Line 163-168 (Saduq).**
Sentence in callout (166): "Rather, we say that revelation which is not Qur'an was sent down ..."
Defect: incomplete beginning. "Rather" answers a sentence that is not shown; the reader does not know what al-Saduq is correcting. Line 168 then restates line 160 ("a total of two kinds of revelation" and "the seventeen thousand verses include everything Jibril brought"), so the same point is made twice.
Action: rewrite the callout opening to start from the preceding clause (source-review p.86-87) or give the denial it answers in an authored lead-in; delete line 160 or line 168.

**R-21. Line 174 and 794: "the opposite conclusion".**
Sentences: "Al-Majlisi graded the report and drew the opposite conclusion." and "Al-Fayd al-Kashani drew the opposite conclusion in the introduction to al-Safi."
Defect: the referent of "opposite" changes between the two uses and in neither is the conclusion stated.
Action: rewrite. State the conclusion drawn: Majlisi reads the report as stating that the Qur'an is deficient; Fayd reads the reports as showing that the Qur'an in hand is incomplete.

**R-22. Line 176-187 (Majlisi in Milani).**
Callout (176-185) and prose (187).
Defects:
(a) Speaker changes inside one paragraph with no marker. The callout opens with Majlisi's own words in quotation marks, then continues in Milani's voice ("What he himself mentioned in "Bihar al-Anwar" ... refutes this"). "He" is Majlisi, "the shaykh of the sect" is al-Tusi, "the traditionist al-Kashani" is al-Fayd, and "the shaykh of the traditionists" is al-Saduq. The reader meets the identity of the last only in the closing lines ("al-Saduq would not have said this").
(b) Incomplete ending: the translation stops mid-sentence at "since the Imamites' proof of it is not confined". The callout begins "Reliable (muwaththaq)." without saying that Majlisi is grading the 17,000-verse report.
(c) Nested quotation: Milani quotes Majlisi, who is quoted inside, who cites Murtada, who is quoted inside, all in double marks.
(d) Prose gloss: "reliable through trustworthy non-Imami narrators" conflicts with the glossary ("trustworthy though some are outside the Imami school").
(e) Prose omits Majlisi's argument. He says that discarding all the loss reports would force the same discarding of the reports on the imamate, which the Imamis accept. The prose says only that "the reports of loss are as numerous as the reports on the imamate". The reader loses why this parity matters.
(f) Milani says Majlisi's own Bihar al-Anwar calls such reports solitary. The article then lists Majlisi among the dissenters (24, 820, 836) without saying that his position is disputed even within the quotation.
Action: rewrite prose (d), (e), (f). Source-review (a)-(c): end the quotation at a complete sentence or add the continuation; label the speaker changes in the layout; name al-Saduq, al-Tusi and al-Fayd where the pronouns stand (layout note, not a translation change).

**R-23. Line 198-202 (Salim ibn Salama report).**
Sentences: "The Imam stops the reading and binds the man to the people's recitation. ... The report shows that Ali's codex differed from the circulating copy, and that the Imam required the circulating recitation in worship."
Defects:
(a) Speakers: in the second block, "And he said" is the Imam, then "He said to them" is Ali, then "They said", then "He said" is Ali again. The block is one paragraph with four speakers.
(b) "shows that Ali's codex differed" overstates. The report shows that a separate codex existed and that the people declined it; the people say they already have one that contains the whole Qur'an. A difference is suggested by the first part, not shown.
(c) "in worship" is not in the report, which says only "recite as the people recite".
Action: rewrite (b) and (c); split the second callout block at each speaker change with a bracketed speaker (layout, source-review). Preserve "It does not say what the difference was".

**R-24. Line 217 (Baqir, Jabir report).**
Sentence: "The report says Ali gathered and preserved it "as God revealed it". The heading reads the claim as knowledge of the Qur'an, its order and its meaning, which the Imams alone hold."
Defects: (a) the quoted phrase does not match the translation, which reads "as God Most High sent it down". (b) The heading (the chapter title) says "knowledge", not "its order and its meaning"; the article adds both. (c) The reader cannot tell whose interpretation this is: the compiler al-Kulayni's chapter title, not a statement by the Imam. (d) The reader is not told why this report threatens the thesis: it says no one but Ali and the Imams collected the whole Qur'an as revealed.
Action: rewrite. Say that al-Kulayni's chapter title reads gathering as knowledge, quote the translation exactly, and state in one clause the implication for the circulating text that the title denies. Source-review "order and meaning".

**R-25. Line 255 (Khoei, Muhammadi, Najashi).**
Sentences: "Al-Khoei names Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari and Ali ibn Ahmad al-Kufi as major sources of these reports. ... He answers them by their meaning."
Defects: "major" is not in the quotation, which says "a number of them" came from al-Sayyari and "others" from al-Kufi. "these reports" and "them" have no clear antecedent after the previous paragraph's Jabir report. "Concedes that the number of reports makes it certain some came from the Imams ... He answers them by their meaning" leaves the reader unsure how weak sources and certain authenticity fit; the connecting step is Khoei's: authentic but not about lost text.
Action: rewrite with exact attribution and the connecting clause.

**R-26. Callout al-Najashi (lines 246-253).**
Defects: (a) incomplete ending: the second paragraph ("Al-Shaykh (70) said ... He was weak") stops mid-sentence and repeats the first paragraph's wording. (b) the footnote marker "(70)" stays in the translation. (c) nested quotation: Najashi's statement contains a quoted chain ("'Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us ... al-Sayyari narrated to me,'") and then ", except for what contained exaggeration and confusion." The reader cannot tell what the "except" clause qualifies: the chain, or the whole of al-Sayyari's books.
Action: source-review. End the quotation at a complete sentence, drop the repeated paragraph and footnote marker, and attach the exception clause to its antecedent.

**R-27. Line 264-270 (Tusi).**
Sentences (270): "He adds that even a sound report of this kind would leave the text between the covers untouched."; callout opening (266) "As for discussing its addition and omission, that too is unsuitable here."
Defects: (a) "solitary reports, which yield neither knowledge nor practice" is unexplained: knowledge means certainty, practice means a basis for legal action. The glossary defines khabar al-wahid but not this phrase, and the abstract uses it first (line 20). (b) The prose drops Tusi's reason why a sound report would not touch the text: the soundness of what lies between the covers is known, and no one in the community objects. Without it the sentence is a bare assertion. (c) The callout begins mid-argument ("that too", "here" are not placed: the discussion is the introduction to a commentary).
Action: rewrite (a) and (b); source-review the callout beginning (add a lead-in sentence saying where in al-Tibyan the passage stands).

**R-28. Line 290 (judging by the Book).**
Sentence: "A report claiming that this Book lost its content would fail the test the Imams set for every report."
Defect: the inference is missing. The test is agreement with the Book. The reader is not told which part of the Book a report of loss contradicts, and may suspect circularity: the rule presupposes the Book in hand is complete. Al-Fayd's argument at line 808 (the loss reports contradict 15:9) gives the bridge but is not stated here. "this Book" has no referent.
Action: rewrite. State the contradiction (the reports of loss contradict the verses that promise the Book's protection, as Fayd says) or state that the rule assumes the Book in hand is the Book. Preserve the Fayd reference.

**R-29. Line 317 (Kafi 2:630-631 paragraph).**
Sentence: "The chain of the third report runs through Sahl ibn Ziyad."
Defect: an incomplete thought. It implies a weakness in the chain but does not say what. It could mislead a reader into a defect that the article does not source.
Action: delete, or complete with the rijal verdict and its source (source-review).

**R-30. Line 317 (purpose of the group).**
Sentence: "Imam al-Baqir places variation in the narrators and keeps the Qur'an one."
Defect: the reader is not told why reports about variant readings bear on the charge of lost text. The inference (the Imams direct followers to the existing text and refuse the seven-ahruf variation) is only partly stated and at line 334.
Action: rewrite with one clause tying the three reports to the question of whether the circulating text is binding.

**R-31. Line 334 (Prophet and Imam compared).**
Sentence: "Both direct the reciter to the transmitted text and away from a private version."
Defect: "a private version" appears in neither report. In the Prophet's report, each man keeps the reading he was taught; in the Imams' reports, followers adopt the common reading. The sentence erases that difference.
Action: rewrite. "The Prophet tells each man to recite as he was taught; the Imam tells the questioner to recite as the people recite." Preserve that both instructions ask for adherence to a received reading.

**R-32. Callout Musnad Abi Ya'la (lines 326-332).**
Sentences in translation: "He said that his face changed, and he said, 'Recite as you were taught.'"; "Then he mentioned some words about it, and then said ..."
Defects: the first sentence renders a direct report of the narrator ("He said: his face changed") as indirect speech, so "he said" is ambiguous between Ibn Mas'ud and the Prophet. In the second block "he mentioned some words" has no subject; the reader assumes the Prophet; the narrator in the Arabic does not recall the words. The speaker changes (Ibn Mas'ud, the two men, the Prophet) are not marked.
Action: source-review the translation of "قال فتغير وجهه فقال" and mark the speakers in layout.

**R-33. Callout Tabataba'i p.108 (lines 341-347) and prose 349.**
Defects: the callout opens "Likewise, the reports show ...", which depends on an unquoted earlier paragraph. The conclusion in the prose, "any difference from Ali's codex lay in the order of suras and verses", turns a conditional ("if ... differs ... it differs only in order") into a finding.
Action: rewrite the prose to keep the conditional; add the preceding sentence or a lead-in to the callout.

## C. Section 5:95 and the commentators

**R-34. Line 363-374 (Hammad's report).**
Sentences: "The report concerns one letter, the alif that makes "one just man" into "two just men". The commentators ask who the kuttab are and what their error was."
Defects:
(a) The reader never sees the two forms: dhu 'adl (one) and dhawa 'adl (two). They are only in the claim bullet, so "alif" has nothing to attach to.
(b) The callout's translation already answers the question the prose then raises: it renders الكتاب as "the scribes", while the next sentence says commentators ask who the kuttab are. The Arabic is unvocalised (الكتاب could be "the Book"), which is the source of the dispute and is not mentioned.
(c) In the translation the sentence "This is one of the things in which the scribes made mistakes" sits outside the quotation marks after "he said, 'a man of justice among you.'" The reader cannot tell if the Imam or Hammad says it. The table (line 41) credits Hammad with reporting that al-Sadiq said it.
(d) The stakes (a report that an Imam said the written text contains a scribal error) appear only at the end of line 414.
Action: rewrite (a), (b) and (d) in authored prose; source-review (b) and (c) in the translation.

**R-35. Callout al-Mazandarani (lines 392-395) and prose 414.**
Sentences: callout "The attribution of error to them is because they made the 'two men of justice' general."; prose "Al-Mazandarani reports the common view, which takes the kuttab as scholars who made the ruling general."
Defects: the callout begins mid-argument ("to them" with no antecedent: kuttab). "Made ... general" is opaque. The reader needs the content of the view: the kuttab read "two just men" as any two just men instead of the Messenger and the Imam. The glossary's "learned men" (line 831) is the only place where this sense of kuttab is stated.
Action: rewrite prose to state the view in plain words. Source-review the callout beginning and the translation of "عمّموا".

**R-36. Callout al-Tabataba'i, Tafsir al-Bayan (lines 397-400).**
Sentence: "The two of them mean the scribes of the codex,"
Defect: incomplete beginning and ending. "The two of them" has no antecedent (al-Baqir and al-Sadiq), and the callout ends with a comma.
Action: source-review. Add the antecedent in a lead-in and end at the completed sentence.

**R-37. Line 414 (four ways).**
Sentences: "The commentators read the report in four ways." ... "Al-Gulpaygani first reads the alif as a scribe's addition, and then judges the dual correct on the strength of Zurara's report. ... Al-Tabrisi records the singular only among the shawadhdh, and the Imams' order to recite as the people recite keeps the dual in recitation."
Defects: (a) the reader cannot match "four ways" to the five scholars named; the copyist reading has two holders and Gulpaygani's first reading repeats it. (b) Tabrisi records the singular as al-Baqir's reading (line 379) while the Zurara report (388) has al-Baqir reciting the dual. The article never says the two attributions to al-Baqir conflict. (c) The final clause uses an inference ("keeps the dual in recitation") that the reader has to reconstruct from the Qa'im report at 198. (d) The paragraph holds five scholars' views and the article's own conclusion with one sentence each, which makes it hard to see which view the article endorses.
Action: rewrite. List the readings by name, state the conflict in al-Baqir's attributions (or source-review it), and say whether the article adopts any view.

## D. Parallel Sunni reports

**R-38. Lines 423-457 (Ibn Abbas group).**
Defects:
(a) The 17:23 item: "the waw became stuck to the sad" cannot be followed without the letters. The Arabic is wassa (و ص ى) against qada (ق ض ى) in unpointed script, and the claim bullet writes "waqada" for wa-qada. The reader sees neither Arabic form.
(b) The Abu Shahba callout begins "They say that" with no identification of the speakers (those who allege tahrif), and ends at "First, these reports are weak and were falsely ascribed" with nothing after "First". The author's own rejection (Abu Shahba says the reports are weak and falsely ascribed) is in the bullet but not stated in prose, so the reader takes the item as support for the parallel without learning that its own source denies it.
(c) The 24:35 item ("the likeness of His light" for "the light of the believer") has no statement of the replacement words or the Arabic. The callout opens on an incomplete verse fragment ("مَثَلُ" and a footnote marker).
(d) The 24:27 item gives "become at ease" and "ask permission" in English. The prose gives no sign that tasta'nisu and tasta'dhinu look alike in the script.
Action: rewrite (a), (c) and (d) with the Arabic words or a clause on the mistake alleged. Rewrite (b): state Abu Shahba's verdict. Source-review the callout ending at "First".

**R-39. Line 457 (three ways).**
Sentence: "Scholars answered these reports in three ways."
Defect: "three ways" does not match the three people because the three are different kinds (forgery, a choice among modes, and interpret-or-reject) and two of the scholars (Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashtah) are not introduced. The reader cannot tell their schools, centuries or relation to Ibn Abbas.
Action: rewrite. One clause of identification for Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashtah.

**R-40. Line 474 (the comparison).**
Sentences: "Sunni scholars graded, interpreted or rejected such reports and held the codex complete. Imami scholars treated the reports in al-Kafi the same way. One standard applied to both bodies of reports gives the same result for each school."
Defects: (a) "graded" is read as "graded sound" for al-Hakim, whose grading (sahih) supports the report and is the opposite of rejecting it; the sentence blends three actions into one verb. (b) "the same way" is false for Majlisi and Fayd, whom the article itself says accepted loss. (c) "One standard" is not named; the reader cannot tell what the standard is. (d) Scale: the Ibn Abbas items are single words; the Kafi reports include a 17,000-verse figure and Fayd's claim of many omissions. The parallel holds for the 5:95 letter only. The article does not state this.
Action: rewrite. Name the standard (a report that contradicts the text the community has is interpreted or rejected) and limit the parallel to the single-word reports. Delete "One standard applied to both bodies of reports gives the same result for each school" unless the standard is stated first.

## E. The Mushaf of Fatimah and Ali's codex

**R-41. Line 478-492 (Mushaf of Fatimah opening).**
Sentence: "Al-Layth defines the mushaf as pages gathered between two boards."
Defect: the section opens with etymology but never states the charge it answers, that the Shia hold a separate Qur'an called the Mushaf of Fatimah. The reader sees a definition with no question. "two boards" in the prose is "two covers" in the quotation.
Action: rewrite. State the charge in one sentence before the definition and use the quotation's wording.

**R-42. Callouts Kafi 1:239-240 (lines 498-533).**
Defects:
(a) Pronoun layering: "He said" stands for the narrator (Abu Basir, Hammad, al-Husayn) in some paragraphs and for the Imam in others. Paragraph pairs read: He said, "I said, 'And what is the Mushaf of Fatima?'" followed by He said, "It is a mushaf ...". The reader cannot tell who "I" or "he" is. The first callout has no isnad and does not name the narrator.
(b) The first callout begins "Then he was silent for a while ... what do they know of the Mushaf of Fatima?" with no antecedent for "they".
(c) In no. 2 the final paragraph reads He said, "Then he said, 'It contains nothing of the lawful and the unlawful ...'". The structure puts the narrator's "then he said" inside the Imam's quotation. It is a nested quotation that misassigns the second "said".
(d) In no. 3 "I do not claim that it contains a Quran": "it" could be the White Jafr or the Mushaf of Fatimah. The White Jafr is never explained.
Action: source-review (a)-(c): label speakers and restructure the nested quotation. Rewrite prose (535) to gloss the White Jafr (source-review) and resolve "it".

**R-43. Line 548 (Kafi 1:64, Ali's writing).**
Sentence: "Imam Ali describes a copy that joined the text to its explanation. ... These belong to teaching about the text."
Defects: (a) the callout is the first half of a sentence (it ends in a comma after "its specific and its general,"), so the reader gets an incomplete ending. (b) The quotation says Ali wrote the verses in his own hand and was taught the interpretation. The article states that he wrote a copy with the explanation. The conclusion "These belong to teaching about the text" is asserted, not shown; the reader cannot tell whether Ali wrote the explanation down.

**R-44. Lines 555-559 (Ihtijaj).**
Sentences: "The refusal concerned a copy that carried the Prophet's arrangement and Ali's notes. ... Al-Mufid identified the missing material as interpretation, and al-Tabataba'i placed the difference in arrangement."
Defects: (a) the first sentence is stated as fact; neither the Ihtijaj report nor the Kafi 1:64 report says "arrangement" or that Ali's notes were in the copy. (b) The two scholars give rival explanations; the article joins them with "and", so the reader cannot tell that they disagree. (c) Mufid in Awa'il al-Maqalat reports a group's view and "inclines toward" it; "identified" is stronger. (d) The callout (557) ends "They said, 'We have no need of it,'" with a comma, so the answer to the refusal is cut, and "them" has no antecedent.

**R-45. Line 565-577 (Nahj al-Balagha).**
Sentences: "During his own caliphate Imam Ali directed people to the Qur'an they held."; "Sermon 156 addresses the people of Basra. Its "Book of God" is the copy in their hands. Imam Ali commends that copy without reservation."
Defects: the quotations say "this Quran" and "the Book of God". The claims that these mean the copy in people's hands and that the addressees are the people of Basra are not in the displayed text. "Without reservation" is the article's gloss. The source line says "without an isnad", and the reader is not told why that matters to the weight of the evidence.

**R-46. Lines 603-608 (Cairo colophon).**
Sentence: "The colophon of the Cairo printing names this chain."
Defect: the quoted text is headed "Introduction to this noble Quran codex" and is not a colophon. "The Cairo printing" does not say which printing, and the source is a modern Shia author's citation (al-Tabrizi), not the printing. The reader cannot check the edition.
Action: rewrite. Name the edition and the source of the quotation (source-review).

**R-47. Line 601 and 624.**
Sentences: "The Hafs reading therefore carries Ali's line."; "One of them is 'arafa without doubling in Qur'an 66:3, which Hafs reads with doubling."
Defects: the first inference depends on the chain only, and "line" needs the word "chain". The second states Hafs's reading with no source in the article; the reader cannot find it in the callouts.

## F. Collection, manuscripts and the Scholars

**R-48. Lines 628-652 (collection).**
Defects: (a) the section never states what charge it answers (that the Companions altered the text when they collected it). The first authored sentence is a fact about Majlisi's copying. **R-49. Lines 654-661 (Uthman via Askari).**
Defects: the callout header packs a chain of speakers (al-Askari, Ahmad, Ibn Abbas, Uthman, the Prophet). The bullet gives "Uthman" only. The speakers inside nested quotes are not marked.

**R-50. Lines 663-676 (Suwayd, Ali on the codices).**
Sentences: "Imam Ali endorses the act of unifying the codices. He kept the Uthmanic codex in use throughout his caliphate."
Defects: (a) the second sentence has no source in the article. (b) The bracket "[Abu Dawud said, from a man, from Suwayd.]" at the end of the callout reports a variant with an unnamed man between Alqama and Suwayd, which may weaken the chain. The reader is not told what the bracket means. (c) The chain in the translation reads "he said, he said, Abu Dawud and Yaqub narrated to us, both said", which looks like duplicated words.

**R-51. Line 684 (manuscripts).**
Sentences: "All fourteen spell ni'mat the same way at the same places." and "The manuscripts are consistent with the reports of an early standard text that displaced the Companions' personal copies."
Defects: (a) the spelling is not stated, so the reader cannot see why identical spelling at identical places points to one archetype (the point: an arbitrary peculiarity copied faithfully). (b) The Sadeghi and Bergmann codex has a non-Uthmanic lower text. That looks like counterevidence to a fixed early text. The article lists it and then says the manuscripts are "consistent with" an early standard text, leaving out the step. (c) "the reports" has no antecedent. (d) The paragraph does not say what the manuscripts show about the question the article asks. They date the text and its common ancestry; they do not show that nothing was lost before that date.

**R-52. Lines 697 (Saduq).**
Sentence: "Al-Saduq also gives the sura count as 114. He treats al-Duha with al-Sharh, and al-Fil with Quraysh, as single suras."
Defect: the quotation says 114 is the count "among the people" and then "we hold" that two pairs are single suras. The prose says al-Saduq "gives" 114 and then counts two pairs as single, which seems to count 112. The reader sees a contradiction and does not learn the Imami count.
Action: rewrite. "Al-Saduq reports that people count 114 suras; the Imamis count al-Duha with al-Sharh and al-Fil with Quraysh as one each." Keep the closing remark that the division does not change the text.

**R-53. Lines 703-729 (Mufid).**
Defects:

Defect class: internal contradiction; equivocation between "Qur'an" and "revelation".
Contribution: the Saduq row of the fact table.
Problem: the Reports in al-Kafi section says Saduq holds that revelation that is not Qur'an was also sent down, large enough that together they total seventeen thousand verses. The quoted I'tiqadat p.86 says the Qur'an is "what lies between the two covers", not that the covers hold everything revealed.
Action: rewrite to "is all of the Qur'an that God sent down". Preserve Saduq's distinction between Qur'an and other revelation.

**R-04. Summary line and Premise 3 / Ibn Abbas parallel. The Sunni-Shia "same treatment" claim is stated as equivalence but the evidence shows different treatments.**
Sentences: "...they treat the reports of loss in their books the way Sunni scholars treat Ibn Abbas's reports of scribal error in theirs." / "One standard applied to both bodies of reports gives the same result for each school." / "Sunni scholars graded, interpreted or rejected such reports and held the codex complete."
Defect class: false analogy; one standard asserted but not shown; verbs not matched to evidence.
Contribution: the comparative argument of the article.
Problem: (a) The Sunni responses in the article are three different moves: al-Hakim accepts the attribution as sahih, Ibn Ashtah reinterprets, Abu Hayyan calls it forgery. The Imami responses are weakening of chains (Khoei), reinterpretation ("thus it was revealed" means explanation) and rejection (Tusi). Those are parallel categories of response, not one standard. (b) The disanalogy of authority is never stated. A scribal-error remark by Ibn Abbas is a Companion's opinion that a Sunni may set aside. The Kafi 5:95 and 2:23 reports are given as speech of infallible Imams, whom the school treats as binding. The Imami scholar therefore cannot discard the content as one man's opinion; he must grade, interpret or reject the report. That is the strongest Sunni objection to the parallel and the article does not state it. (c) The Sunni reports chosen (single-word scribal slips) are lighter than the Kafi reports chosen (seventeen thousand verses; "thus it was revealed" with Ali's name). The weightier Sunni parallel is the set of reports of lost verses and abrogated recitation (the stoning verse; the length of Surat al-Ahzab; Ubayy's additional surahs), which the article does not mention. Without it the parallel covers only the 5:95 report.
Action: rewrite the summary and the sentence in "Parallel Reports". Preserve: both bodies of reports were met with grading, interpretation or rejection. State the authority difference in one sentence. Either add the heavier Sunni parallel (needs a primary source, source-review) or narrow the claim to "reports of scribal error".

**R-05. Reports in al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir report, no.1. The heading is credited with a reading it does not state.**
Sentence: "The heading reads the claim as knowledge of the Qur'an, its order and its meaning, which the Imams alone hold."
Defect class: misattributed inference; speculation presented as the source's reading.
Contribution: the only answer to the report that only Ali and the Imams collected the Qur'an "as God sent it down".
Problem: the chapter heading says "no one collected the whole Qur'an except the Imams, and they know all its knowledge". It joins two clauses and does not redefine "collected" as "knew". The word "order" is in neither the heading nor the report. This is the author's reading, given as the heading's. The Sunni objection is direct: the report says the Qur'an "as God sent it down" exists only with the Imams, which is what Mufid's and Fayd's "complete Qur'an with its rightful people" holds. The article also puts "as God revealed it" in quotation marks, but its own translation reads "as God Most High sent it down".
Action: rewrite. Preserve: the report says no one but Ali and the Imams collected and memorised it as sent down. Attribute the explanatory reading to a named commentator (source-review for one) or state it as the author's reading and say what the report plainly implies about the text in circulation. Fix the quotation marks.

**R-06. Reports in al-Kafi, 2:23. The chapter title is used as evidence for the reading it does not support.**
Sentence: "Al-Kulayni titled their chapter "points from the tanzil", and tanzil can mean the occasion and sense of revelation."
Defect class: non sequitur; unsourced lexical claim; authorial intention inferred from a title.
Contribution: the bridge from "thus it was revealed" to "explanation".
Problem: the report says Gabriel came down "with this verse in this form". Kulayni's title ("points and fragments from the tanzil concerning wilaya") read plainly names revelation, so it is at least as consistent with the literal reading. What Kulayni meant is unrecorded in the article. The explanatory reading rests on Tabataba'i's argument (which the next sentence cites) and on Fayd's p.55 passage. Khoei, in the article, concedes some reliable reports still say "thus it was revealed". The glossary repeats the unsourced sense of tanzil.
Action: delete the Kulayni sentence; keep the Tabataba'i sentence and state that the reading is his. Add a lexicon source for the glossary sense or delete it from the glossary (source-review).

**R-07. Mufid sections. The article's summaries of Mufid disagree with each other and omit his concession on addition.**
Sentences: "Al-Mufid identified the missing material as interpretation, and al-Tabataba'i placed the difference in arrangement." (Ali's Codex section) / "he preferred the view that only interpretation was dropped" (claim line) / "Neither work dates itself relative to the other."
Defect class: internal inconsistency; counterevidence omitted.
Contribution: Mufid's position anchors the answer to the "Ali's codex" objection.
Problem: (a) In Sarawiyya (pp.78-79) Mufid says what lies between the covers is the "majority" of what was revealed, that the collector left some of it out for stated reasons including "deliberate exclusion", and that the rest is with the guardian of the law. That is not interpretation dropped. The Ali's Codex sentence gives only the Awa'il view. (b) In Awa'il (quoted on the page) Mufid says that "a word, two words, a letter, two letters" might have been added and could be mistaken for Qur'anic speech by most eloquent people; the article's summary does not mention it. This bears directly on Premise 2 ("addition is false by consensus") and on the 5:95 copyist reading. (c) Mufid's inclination in Awa'il is that the Qur'an is safe from loss, and he adds that the opposite was held by the Banu Nawbakht and a group of theologians and jurists (see R-01). (d) The article never states the sharpest form of the Sunni objection from Mufid: that a leading early Imami scholar describes the codex as the majority of the revelation, with the remainder held by the Imam.
Action: rewrite the Ali's Codex sentence to "In Awa'il al-Maqalat al-Mufid reports a view that the missing material was interpretation, and in al-Sarawiyya he says the collector left material out". Add Mufid's word-and-letter addition concession to the Mufid paragraph. Source-review whether the Awa'il text continues to qualify it (the capture ends mid-sentence).

**R-08. Premise 2 and Glossary. "Muslims dispute only one of them" is Khoei's claim, presented as established fact, and the article tests it against nothing.**
Sentences: "Al-Khoei lists six senses of the word, and Muslims dispute only one of them, the loss of revealed text." / "A report that speaks of tahrif may therefore mean a false interpretation. A charge of tahrif has to show that the report means lost text."
Defect class: authorial position stated as historical fact; hidden premise; possible internal conflict.
Contribution: the definition on which the article sorts the 5:95 and 2:23 reports.
Problem: (a) Only senses 1, 5 and 6 are quoted. Senses 2 to 4 (as I recall Khoei, changes of letters or vowels or a word while the Qur'an stays intact) are not in the article, so the reader cannot check "only one". (b) Sense 5 is "addition ... part of the codex in our hands is not revealed speech", false by consensus. On the copyist reading of the 5:95 report, which the article gives for Mazandarani ("clearer"), Tabataba'i and Gulpaygani, the alif is a scribal addition. That is sense 5 or a neighbour of it, held by commentators in the school. Either the report falls in a sense Khoei excludes, or it falls in sense 2 to 4 and the article should say so. As written, the article cannot say both "only loss is disputed" and "the Imams called one letter a scribal addition". (c) "A charge of tahrif has to show that the report means lost text" assigns the burden by definition; a Sunni critic will answer that the 5:95 report on its most natural reading means a changed letter in the text.
Action: source-review Khoei pp.198-199 for senses 2 to 4 and state where the one-letter scribal-error reading falls. Rewrite Premise 2 to "Al-Khoei says Muslims dispute only one of them". Rewrite or delete the burden sentence.

## B. Inference and scope defects

**R-09. The Charge Ibn Hazm Recorded. Two conclusions go beyond Ibn Hazm's text.**
Sentence: "The charge therefore described some Imami transmitters, and its author knew that the school's chief scholar rejected it."
Defect class: non sequitur; imputes knowledge; asserts what the exception does not show.
Contribution: the article's reading of Ibn Hazm's exception.
Problem: Ibn Hazm exempts three named people. That shows he knew of them. It does not show that the charge "described some Imami transmitters", a claim for which no evidence is given. "Chief scholar" is the author's rank assignment. Premise 1 also says Ibn Hazm exempted al-Murtada "by name", but the text gives "Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Musa ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Musa ibn Jafar ..." (al-Hasan, not al-Husayn; one Musa omitted). Identification with al-Murtada is an inference from the genealogy and the Mu'tazili tendency. A Sunni objection: a heresiographer's blanket statement with three exceptions is still a testimony that the doctrine was general; the exceptions are what the article must explain.
Action: rewrite. Preserve: Ibn Hazm made a blanket charge and exempted three; the first is described as an Imami with Mu'tazili leanings who called holders of the view unbelievers. State that the identification with al-Murtada is an inference (source-review: a scholarly identification). Delete "its author knew ...".

**R-10. The Guarantee of Qur'an 15:9. The heading and table claim a verse guarantee that the cited passage does not argue from.**
Sentences: heading "The Guarantee of Qur'an 15:9"; table "The Qur'an keeps every attribute God gave it, so no loss touches its substance"; "A change in wording or order would remove those effects."
Defect class: scope shift; imported premise; unqualified paraphrase.
Contribution: the verse-based part of the case.
Problem: (a) Tabataba'i's quoted argument is from the Qur'an's attributes (inimitability, guidance), using "a preserved Reminder" as a label. It does not interpret 15:9 itself. The article does not state the two inferences needed to use the verse: that dhikr means the Qur'an text and that "guardians" means preservation of its wording. It also does not mention the circularity objection to proving the text's integrity from a verse in that text, which a sceptic and some Imamis (the 15:9-circularity argument) raise. (b) The sentence "A change in wording or order would remove those effects" drops Tabataba'i's qualifier ("that affects it") and is contradicted two sentences later. (c) The table row says "no loss touches its substance"; the passage itself concedes a lost repeated verse or a changed dot. "Substance" hides the concession.
Action: rewrite (a) to say what Tabataba'i argues from; keep 15:9 as the verse he cites; add one sentence on the circularity limit if a source states it (source-review). Rewrite (b) as "A change that affected those attributes would show in them." Rewrite (c) as "A change that leaves those attributes intact is not excluded." Preserve the author's already correct limit.

**R-11. Reports in al-Kafi, no.28. The Saduq reading and the Majlisi block are not weighed against the report's wording.**
Sentences: "Al-Saduq gives the same figure as the report and assigns the excess to non-Qur'anic revelation." / "Al-Majlisi's reading is a recorded Imami position, and the school's leading scholars rejected it."
Defect class: unaddressed objection; third-hand source for an attribution.
Contribution: the answer to the main loss report.
Problem: (a) The report says "the Qur'an that Gabriel brought", not "revelation". Saduq's reading replaces the word. The Sunni objection (the report speaks of Qur'an) and the size implied (about ten thousand verses of non-Qur'anic revelation, more than one and a half times the Qur'an) are not stated. (b) Majlisi's text is quoted through al-Milani, who is arguing against him, and the capture (`s-majlisi-intisar.json`) shows a second hostile source, al-Amili, with the same passage and Majlisi's note that one copy reads Hisham ibn Salim, "so the report is sound". Milani's counter that Majlisi elsewhere calls such reports solitary is reported, but the Final Verdict presents "al-Majlisi read some reports as proof of loss" without that qualifier. Majlisi's own position is therefore internally contested in the article's own sources. (c) "As numerous as the reports on the imamate" misstates "no less than" (la yaqsur) and turns a strength-of-evidence claim into a quantity claim.
Action: rewrite (c) to "no weaker than the reports that establish the imamate". Add to Premise 5 and the verdict that Majlisi is known here through a critic and a dispute over his own consistency. Add a sentence on why Saduq's change of "Qur'an" to "revelation" is an interpretation (source-review for Saduq's own grounds in wahy2 capture).

**R-12. Majlisi dilemma left unanswered.**
Sentence in block (quoted, not authored): "discarding all of them would remove reliance on reports altogether... the reports on this subject are no less than the reports on the imamate".
Defect class: strongest internal objection not answered by an authored sentence.
Contribution: the strongest Imami argument for loss and a Sunni talking point.
Problem: the article reports Milani's reply (accepting all would also remove reliance) but does not state the structure: if Imami grading rejects the loss reports as solitary, the same grading is applied to every other report in the same books, including those the article itself relies on (Mushaf of Fatimah, "recite as you were taught", "present to the Book"). The article uses Kafi reports selectively without saying what criterion separates them. Tusi's phrase "solitary reports that yield neither knowledge nor practice" is also in tension with the school's practice of acting on solitary reports in law, which a Sunni critic will raise.
Action: add one authored sentence that states the criterion the school applies (chain grade, agreement with the Book, mutawatir support), source-review for a school source that states it (Khoei, Mu'jam or al-Bayan). Preserve all quotations.

**R-13. How the School Weighs a Solitary Report. The "present to the Book" argument proves less than stated.**
Sentence: "A report claiming that this Book lost its content would fail the test the Imams ﵈ set for every report."
Defect class: invalid inference (omission vs alteration); circularity.
Contribution: the rule-based argument against loss reports.
Problem: the test asks whether a report agrees or disagrees with the Book in hand. A report that verses are missing does not contradict anything in the Book; Tusi says as much ("even if they were sound that would be no challenge to what exists"). The test defeats reports of alteration (a changed verse, 2:23 with "concerning Ali") and Fayd's "every verse could be altered" argument, not reports of omission. The test is also itself conveyed by reports, so it is subject to the same grading. The article transfers Fayd's argument against alteration to the loss reports.
Action: rewrite. Preserve: the rule presupposes that the Book in hand is authentic and consultable. Limit the conclusion to reports of alteration and say that Tusi's separate argument covers omission.

**R-14. "Recite as the people recite" is read as endorsement of completeness.**
Sentences: "The Imams ﵈ bound their followers to the people's recitation." / "Both direct the reciter to the transmitted text and away from a private version."
Defect class: ambiguous middle; counterevidence in the same report.
Contribution: Premise 4 and Final Verdict.
Problem: Kafi no.23 says "recite as the people recite until the Qa'im rises, ... he will recite the Book of God by itself". The instruction is time-limited and implies that the Qa'im's recitation will differ. Mufid cites the same order as compatible with his view that the codex is not the complete revelation. An obligation to recite the circulating text shows that it is the text of worship and law, not that it is complete. The article states the limit once ("does not say what the difference was") and then uses the instruction as proof of preservation. The Prophet-instruction comparison (Musnad Abi Ya'la) is an instruction on two authorised readings and is a different kind of statement.
Action: rewrite the two sentences to say what the instruction shows (the circulating text is binding for recitation and law now) and that the Imami scholars who read it as proof of completeness (Tabataba'i, Mufid for obligation only) differ. Delete the sentence comparing the two instructions unless the comparison is sourced.

**R-15. The Sahl ibn Ziyad sentence gives a fact without its consequence.**
Sentence: "The chain of the third report runs through Sahl ibn Ziyad."
Defect class: unexplained inference; reader loses the point.
Contribution: a disclosure of a grading weakness, no stated implication.
Problem: the reader is not told that Sahl ibn Ziyad is disputed in the rijal literature, nor which scholar accepts him. The following sentence ("The same instruction appears in the report of Salim ibn Salama above") is the implied rescue, but Salim ibn Salama's chain is not graded either. The article grades Kafi reports of loss by chain and does not grade the Kafi reports it relies on.
Action: source-review the rijal verdicts for Sahl ibn Ziyad and for the Salim ibn Salama chain; rewrite to state them, or delete the Sahl sentence.

**R-16. Hammad's Report on Qur'an 5:95. The reading with the largest weight in the cited commentators is answered by a lighter argument.**
Sentences: "On the copyist reading, the report alleges a one-letter error of the kind the Sunni reports below attribute to Ibn Abbas. Al-Tabrisi records the singular only among the shawadhdh, and the Imams' ﵈ order to recite as the people recite keeps the dual in recitation."
Defect class: unaddressed objection; analogy of unequal authority; weak closing inference.
Contribution: the article's answer to the most concrete report of scribal error in al-Kafi.
Problem: three of the four commentators the article lists (Mazandarani, Tabataba'i, and Gulpaygani's first reading) take the Imam to mean that the copyists erred. The article treats this as one of four readings; the weights are not equal. If an infallible Imam says the codex has a scribal error, the school holds that the circulating codex has at least one letter that is not revelation. That is the Sunni objection, and the article responds with the parallel to Ibn Abbas (R-04 shows the parallel has no equal authority) and with the practical instruction, which does not touch the claim. Gulpaygani's second move relies on the Ayyashi report that explains the dual, and it is an interpretation of the Imam's saying that the Imam's own words in Kafi do not suggest.
Action: rewrite. State plainly that on the readings of Mazandarani and Tabataba'i the Imam says the codex has an added alif, state the school's practical rule, and say that Gulpaygani and Fayd read the Imam otherwise. Preserve all four readings and the shawadhdh point. Do not claim more than "reports in al-Kafi and commentators differ".

**R-17. Parallel Reports in Sunni Books. Secondary and hostile sources stand in for the Sunni primary reports.**
Sentences: heading; "Sunni books carry reports in which a Companion calls a word of the codex a scribe's mistake." (and 17:23 block from Abu Shahba)
Defect class: secondhand evidence; source-boundary.
Contribution: the evidence for the Sunni parallel.
Problem: the 24:27 report (Hakim) and the 24:35 report (Ibn Abi Hatim) are primary. The 17:23 report comes from Abu Shahba, a modern defender who says the reports are "weak and falsely ascribed", and who reports the claim as "they say". The article also uses Abu Hayyan only through Abu Shahba. The sentence "Sunni books carry reports ..." is supported for two of three examples. Hakim is also known as lenient in grading, and Dhahabi's reaction in the Talkhis to this report is not given, so "graded sahih" is a weaker datum than the article makes it. The capture list holds `r-tabari-24-27.json` and `r-itqan-17-23-a.json`, so the primary locators for 17:23 may be available.
Action: source-review. Replace the Abu Shahba block with the primary report (Tabari or al-Itqan) or label it as a secondary report. Add Dhahabi's comment on Hakim's grade if present.

**R-18. Ali's Codex and His Teaching. Two unsourced characterisations of the codex.**
Sentences: "Imam Ali ﵇ describes a copy that joined the text to its explanation." / "The refusal concerned a copy that carried the Prophet's ﷺ arrangement and Ali's ﵇ notes."
Defect class: assertion beyond the quoted text.
Contribution: the account of what Ali's codex was.
Problem: the Kafi text (p.64) says the Prophet dictated each verse to Ali, who wrote it, and taught him its interpretation, abrogation and the like. It does not say that the written copy contained the interpretation. The Ihtijaj text says he swore to gather the Qur'an and presented it. Neither mentions the Prophet's "arrangement" or "notes". The next sentence then reports two Imami views (Mufid, Tabataba'i) that disagree with each other. The first sentence states as fact what the two views dispute.
Action: rewrite. Preserve: the reports say Ali wrote the Qur'an at the Prophet's dictation and was taught its interpretation; the sources differ on what the refused copy contained (interpretation, per one Mufid view; order, per Tabataba'i; unspecified material left out, per Mufid in Sarawiyya). Delete "carried the Prophet's arrangement and Ali's notes".

**R-19. Nahj al-Balagha paragraph. The evidence is weak and the inference strong.**
Sentences: "Sermon 156 addresses the people of Basra. Its "Book of God" is the copy in their hands. Imam Ali ﵇ commends that copy without reservation."
Defect class: overreach; authenticity omitted; misidentification risk.
Contribution: Ali endorses the circulating Qur'an.
Problem: the sermons praise the Qur'an ("this Qur'an", "the Book of God") in terms that apply equally to the Qur'an as revelation. Mufid, Tabataba'i and even Fayd hold these sermons compatible with a different arrangement or with extra interpretation in Ali's codex. "Is the copy in their hands" and "without reservation" are the author's inferences. The article says the sermons have no isnad, but does not say that the Nahj's attribution is disputed by Sunni critics (a standard Sunni objection to using it). Whether sermon 156 was addressed to the people of Basra is stated without a source (source-review).
Action: rewrite to "praise the Qur'an in terms that fit the text he told his hearers to follow". Delete "without reservation" and "Its 'Book of God' is the copy in their hands". Source-review the Basra claim.

**R-20. Ali's Reading in the Printed Mushaf. The inference contradicts the article's own examples and rests on a disputed chain.**
Sentences: "The Hafs reading therefore carries Ali's ﵇ line." / "Ali's ﵇ variants of this kind sit inside the accepted readings and share one consonant skeleton with them."
Defect class: contradiction with own evidence; chain reliability; the colophon is not independent evidence.
Contribution: the claim that the printed mushaf transmits Ali's reading.
Problem: (a) The article says Shu'ba "introduced ten letters" from Ali's reading into Asim's reading, and that Hafs reads the first of them (66:3) with doubling where Ali's reading has none. If Hafs already carried Ali's reading, Shu'ba would not need to import it, and the 66:3 example shows Hafs differing from Ali's reading. The 6:159 example concerns Hamza and al-Kisa'i, not Hafs. The section's own evidence shows that Ali's variants exist in other canonical readings and that Hafs differs from them. The sentence "therefore carries Ali's line" is a statement about a chain, not about the text, and the article's examples refute the textual version. (b) The Dhahabi chain runs through Amr ibn al-Sabbah, whom the rijal literature criticises (to be verified; source-review); the article gives no grade. (c) The colophon of the Cairo printing is a modern editorial statement by the printers and cannot corroborate the chain. (d) "Share one consonant skeleton" is true of the 6:159 and 66:3 pairs only if the skeleton is shown; the 5:95 variant (dhu / dhawa) differs by an alif, and the article does not claim it shares the skeleton.
Action: rewrite to "Dhahabi reports a chain from Hafs through Asim and al-Sulami to Ali. Shu'ba's and al-Shawkani's examples show that Ali's variants survive in canonical readings, and that Hafs does not always follow them." Delete the colophon block or label it as a modern editorial attribution. Source-review Amr ibn al-Sabbah.

**R-21. Collection in the Shia Sources. Absence of comment is read as acceptance.**
Sentence: "Al-Majlisi labels the report as al-Bukhari's and al-Tirmidhi's. He presents it without a charge of loss."
Defect class: argument from silence; selective excerpt.
Contribution: that Imami scholars accepted the Sunni collection account.
Problem: the excerpt ends at the transmission of the sheets to Hafsa. Majlisi's Bihar often places such reports beside others that contradict them, so what follows and what he says elsewhere cannot be inferred from the excerpt. A compiler who records a report is not endorsing it. The section is also headed "Collection in the Shia Sources", which promises a Shia position that the excerpt does not supply. The second item (Musnad Ahmad via al-Askari) is a Sunni report cited by an Imami author and says the Prophet told scribes where to place verses; the article's inference "The order of verses within suras therefore goes back to the Prophet" extends a single report to all verses, and Tabataba'i (quoted earlier) allows that the order of "some verses" may differ from Ali's.
Action: source-review the next lines of Bihar 89 p.76. Delete the "without a charge of loss" sentence unless a source shows endorsement. Rewrite the Musnad Ahmad sentence to "by this report, the Prophet told his scribes where to place the verses revealed in his time" and drop "therefore ... order of verses within suras".

**R-22. Ali's statement on the codices. An unsourced historical fact.**
Sentence: "He kept the Uthmanic codex in use throughout his caliphate."
Defect class: unsourced historical claim; inference from silence.
Contribution: the second half of the argument for Ali's endorsement.
Problem: no citation for the practice; the first sentence ("endorses the act of unifying the codices") is a reading of an ambiguous report with a chain flaw the article itself reproduces ("Abu Dawud said, from a man, from Suwayd").
Action: source-review. Delete the sentence or give its source; attribute the first sentence ("the report has Ali saying ...").

**R-23. The Earliest Manuscripts. Relevance and strength of the manuscript claims.**
Sentences: "Radiocarbon tests placed the parchment of the two Birmingham leaves between 568 and 645 CE, with 95 per cent probability." / "He argues that they descend from a single written archetype made within the first century." / "The manuscripts are consistent with the reports of an early standard text that displaced the Companions' personal copies." Claim line: "the earliest copies date close to the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime and descend from one written archetype".
Defect class: authorial position stated as the section's established claim; relevance not tied to the dispute; counterevidence compressed.
Contribution: external, non-Islamic-source evidence of an early fixed text.
Problem: (a) The claim line states as fact what van Putten "argues". (b) Radiocarbon dates the animal skin, not the writing; the range begins about two years before the Prophet's birth. The article states the date accurately but the claim line "close to the Prophet's lifetime" omits the limit. (c) The section never says what it shows for the Sunni-Shia question: a single archetype shows early standardisation, and says nothing about loss before it or about whether the Imami scholars' text matches. (d) The Sadeghi-Bergmann lower text is non-Uthmanic and is described as the "only known manuscript of that kind". It is evidence that a variant text existed. The article's last sentence takes it as "consistent with" the displacement report. That is accurate, but the same fact supports a Companion-codex reading (Ibn Mas'ud) that Imami and Sunni sources both record, so it cuts against the claim that no text variation existed.
Action: rewrite the claim line to "the earliest dated parchment falls in or near the Prophet's lifetime, and one study argues for a single archetype". Add the sentence stating what the evidence does and does not show (an early standard text; no information on lost text before it). Delete the section if the economy reviewer finds it does not bear on the charge.

**R-24. Murtada, Tabrisi and Khoei blocks. Argument by scale and by insult stated without scope.**
Sentences: "A community that careful could not lose verses without knowing it." / (Khoei p.259 quotation, with no authored comment.)
Defect class: argument by assertion; authorial inference without source limit; ad hominem inside a source.
Contribution: Murtada's tawatur argument; Khoei's rejection.
Problem: (a) Murtada argues that care for the text rules out loss. The article's gloss turns his "how can it be ..." into a flat deduction. The Sunni objection is the same argument made by Sunni scholars about their own sources (so the argument does not distinguish the schools), which is fine for the article's aim but should be stated, because the argument also covers the Sunni reports of lost verses. (b) The Khoei p.259 passage calls those who hold the loss view weak-minded; Majlisi, Fayd and (by Khomeini) Nuri are among them. The article quotes it with no comment and then calls them a minority of scholars. The quotation records Khoei's attitude; it adds no argument.
Action: rewrite (a) to attribute the inference to Murtada and name the shared consequence. Delete the Khoei p.259 block or add one sentence on what it adds.

## C. Lower-weight reasoning notes

**R-25. Fayd al-Kashani paragraph. The closing sentence mixes a count claim and an inference.**
Sentence: "Al-Fayd in al-Safi and al-Majlisi represent the Imami minority, and the scholars above reject their reading."
Defect class: scope; unqualified count; also repeats the Final Verdict.
Contribution: restates the conclusion; the facts (Fayd's position and his own answer) are in the preceding sentences.
Problem: Fayd's "final answer" (the complete Qur'an is preserved with its rightful people and the community holds what it needs) is the same position as Mufid's Sarawiyya. The article treats it as a minority view and does not say it matches the Mufid text it summarised earlier. paragraphs.text: فقد تبين مما فصلناه ان القرآن الذي أنزله الله على نبيه ﵌ ووصفه بأنه ذكر محفوظ على ما انزل مصون بصيانة الهية عن الزيادة والنقيصة والتغيير كما وعد الله نبيه فيه . وخلاصة الحجة ان القرآن أنزله الله على نبيه ووصفه في آيات كثيرة بأوصاف خاصة لو كان تغير في شئ من هذه الأوصاف بزيادة أو نقيصة أو تغيير في لفظ أو ترتيب مؤثر فقد آثار تلك الصفة قطعا لكنا نجد القرآن الذي بأيدينا واجدا لاثار تلك الصفات المعدودة على أتم ما يمكن وأحسن ما يكون فلم يقع فيه تحريف يسلبه شيئا من صفاته فالذي بأيدينا منه هو القرآن المنزل على النبي ﵌ بعينه فلو فرض سقوط شئ منه أو تغير في اعراب أو حرف أو ترتيب وجب ان يكون في أمر لا يؤثر في شئ من أوصافه كالاعجاز وارتفاع الاختلاف والهداية والنورية والذكرية والهيمنة على سائر الكتب السماوية إلى غير ذلك وذلك كآية مكررة ساقطة أو اختلاف في نقطة أو اعراب ونحوها .

What we have set out shows that the Qur'an which God sent down to his Prophet, and which he described as a preserved Reminder, remains as it was sent down. It is protected by divine safeguarding from addition, omission and alteration, as God promised his Prophet in it.

The summary of the argument is this. God sent the Qur'an down to his Prophet and described it in many verses with particular attributes. If any of these attributes had changed through addition, omission, or a change in a word or in an order that affects it, the traces of that attribute would certainly have been affected. Yet we find that the Qur'an in our hands carries the traces of those enumerated attributes to the fullest extent possible and in the best form. So no tahrif has occurred in it that strips it of any of its attributes. What we have of it is therefore the very Qur'an that was sent down to the Prophet.

If we suppose that something dropped out of it, or that a vowel ending, a letter or an order changed, then it must have been in a matter that affects none of its attributes. Those attributes include its inimitability, the absence of discrepancy in it, its guidance, its luminosity, its being a reminder, and its authority over the other heavenly books, and so on. An example is a repeated verse that dropped out, or a difference in a dot or a vowel ending, and the like.

paragraphs.text: 2 - الشيخ المجلسي في كتابه ( مرآة العقول ) فإنّه قال بعد حديث قال إنّه موثق : « ولا يخفى أنّ هذا الخبر وكثير من الأخبار الصحيحة صريحة في نقص القرآن وتغييره . وعندي أنّ الأخبار في هذا الباب متواترة معنىً ، وطرح جميعها يوجب رفع الاعتماد على الأخبار رأساً ، بل ظنّي أنّ الأخبار في هذا الباب لا تقصر عن أخبار الإمامة ، فكيف يثبتونها بالخبر » . ويردّه ما ذكره هو في « بحار الأنوار » وقد تقدّم نصّة . على أنّ قوله : « وكثير من الأخبار الصحيحة صريحة في نقص القرآن » غريب ، فإنّ السيد المرتضى قال : « نقلوا أخباراً ضعيفة ظنّوا صحتها لا يرجع بمثلها عن المعلوم المقطوع على صحته » . كما أنكر صحتها الطوسي شيخ الطائفة والمحدّث الكاشاني ، بل جاء في العبارة التي نقلناها عن بحاره « إنّ الأخبار التي جاءت بذلك أخبار آحاد لا يقطع على الله تعالى بصحّتها » . ومن قبلهم قال شيخ المحدّثين ما نصّه : « إعتقادنا أنّ القرآن الذين أنزله الله على نبيّه ﵌ هو ما بين الدفّتين وما في أيدي الناس ، ليس بأكثر من ذاك . . . ومن نسب إلينا أنّا نقول إنّه أكثر من ذلك فهو كاذب » . ولو كانت أحاديث النقيصة صحيحة ومقبولة لما قال الصدوق ذلك كما لا يخفى . وأما قوله : « وطرح جميعها يوجب رفع الاعتماد على الأخبار رأساً » ففيه : إنّ قبول جميعها أيضاً يوجب رفع الاعتماد على الأحاديث رأساً ، على أنّه رحمة الله قد حكم في أكثر الأحاديث المخرّجة في « الكافي » والمفيدة نقص القرآن إمّا بالضعف وإمّا بالإرسال ، كما تقدّم ذلك كلّه . ومن العجيب قوله : « بل ظنّي . . . » إذ إثبات الإمامية ليس دليلة منحصراً بالأحاديث حتى يقال ذلك ، وكيف أنّ تلك الأحاديث لا تقصر عن أحاديث الإمامة ؟ وهل يقصد الكثرة في الورود ؟ أو القوة في الدلالة ؟ أو الصحة في الأسانيد ؟

2. Al-Shaykh al-Majlisi, in his book Mir'at al-'Uqul, said after a hadith that he called reliable, "It is not hidden that this report and many sound reports are explicit about the diminution and alteration of the Quran. In my view the reports on this subject are mutawatir in meaning, and rejecting all of them would remove reliance on reports altogether. Rather, I think the reports on this subject fall no shorter than the reports on the Imamate, so how can they establish the Imamate by a report?" What he himself mentioned in Bihar al-Anwar refutes this, and its text has already been given.

Moreover, his statement "many sound reports are explicit about the diminution of the Quran" is strange, because al-Sayyid al-Murtada said, "They transmitted weak reports that they thought were sound, and one does not turn away from what is known and certain to be sound because of the like of these." Al-Tusi, the Shaykh of the sect, and the hadith scholar al-Kashani likewise denied their soundness. Indeed, the passage we quoted from his Bihar says, "The reports that came about this are solitary reports (ahad), and their soundness cannot be affirmed with certainty about God Most High." Before them, the Shaykh of the hadith scholars said, in these words, "Our belief is that the Quran which God sent down to His Prophet is what is between the two covers and in the hands of the people, and it is no more than that... Whoever attributes to us that we say it is more than that is a liar." Had the hadiths of diminution been sound and accepted, al-Saduq would not have said this, as is clear.

As for his statement "rejecting all of them would remove reliance on reports altogether," the reply is that accepting all of them would also remove reliance on hadiths altogether. Moreover, may God have mercy on him, he judged most of the hadiths cited in al-Kafi that indicate diminution of the Quran to be either weak or mursal, as all of that has been shown earlier. His statement "Rather, I think..." is also remarkable, since the proof of the Imamate is not confined to hadiths, so that this could be said. And how do those hadiths fall no shorter than the hadiths of the Imamate? Does he mean abundance in transmission, strength in indication, or soundness in the chains of transmission?

paragraphs.text: 23 - محمد بن يحيى ، عن محمد بن الحسين ، عن عبد الرحمن بن أبي هاشم ، عن سالم بن سلمة قال : قرأ رجل على أبي عبد الله (﵇) وأنا أستمع حروفا من القرآن ليس على ما يقرؤها الناس ، فقال أبو عبد الله (﵇) : كف عن هذه القراءة اقرأ كما يقرأ الناس حتى يقوم القائم فإذا قام القائم (﵇) قرأ كتاب الله ﷿ على حده وأخرج المصحف الذي كتبه علي (﵇) وقال : أخرجه علي (﵇) إلى الناس حين فرغ منه وكتبه فقال لهم : هذا كتاب الله ﷿ كما أنزله [الله] على محمد (﵌) وقد جمعته من اللوحين فقالوا : هو ذا عندنا مصحف جامع فيه القرآن لا حاجة لنا فيه ، فقال أما والله ما ترونه بعد يومكم هذا أبدا ، إنما كان علي أن أخبركم حين جمعته لتقرؤوه .
23. Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim, from Salim ibn Salama, who said.

A man recited to Abu Abd Allah, while I was listening, some letters of the Qur'an that were not as the people recite them. Abu Abd Allah said, “Stop this recitation. Recite as the people recite until the Qa'im rises. When the Qa'im rises, he will recite the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, by itself, and he will bring out the codex that Ali wrote.”

And he said, “Ali brought it out to the people when he had finished it and written it. He said to them, ‘This is the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, as [God] sent it down to Muhammad, and I have gathered it from the two tablets.’ They said, ‘Here with us is a codex that contains the whole Qur'an, and we have no need of it.’ He said, ‘By God, you will never see it after this day of yours. It was only my duty to inform you, when I had gathered it, so that you would recite it.’”

paragraphs.text: (باب) (انه لم يجمع القرآن كله الا الأئمة ﵈ وانهم) (يعلمون علمه كله) 1 - محمد بن يحيى ، عن أحمد بن محمد ، عن ابن محبوب ، عن عمرو بن أبي المقدام عن جابر قال : سمعت أبا جعفر ﵇ يقول : ما ادعى أحد من الناس أنه جمع القرآن كله كما أنزل إلا كذاب ، وما جمعه وحفظه كما نزله الله تعالى إلا علي بن أبي طالب ﵇ والأئمة من بعده ﵈ .
Chapter. That no one collected the whole Quran except the Imams, and that they know all of its knowledge.
1 - Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Amr ibn Abi al-Miqdam, from Jabir, who said that he heard Abu Ja'far say,

“No one among the people claims that he collected the whole Quran as it was sent down, except a liar. No one collected it and memorized it as God Most High sent it down except Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Imams after him.”

paragraphs.text: والجواب : أن هذه الروايات لا دلالة فيها على وقوع التحريف في القرآن بالمعنى المتنازع فيه ، وتوضيح ذلك : أن كثيرا من الروايات ، وإن كانت ضعيفة السند ، فإن جملة منها نقلت من كتاب أحمد بن محمد السياري ، الذي اتفق علماء الرجال على فساد مذهبه ، وأنه يقول بالتناسخ ، ومن علي بن أحمد الكوفي الذي ذكر علماء الرجال أنه كذاب ، وأنه فاسد المذهب إلا أن كثرة الروايات تورث القطع بصدور بعضها عن المعصومين ﵈ ولا أقل من الاطمئنان بذلك ، وفيها ما روي بطريق معتبر فلا حاجة بنا إلى التكلم في سند كل رواية بخصوصها .

The answer is that these reports give no indication that distortion occurred in the Quran in the sense under dispute. To explain this, many of the reports have weak chains of transmission. A number of them were transmitted from the book of Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari, whose doctrine the scholars of biographical evaluation agreed was corrupt, and who held the belief in transmigration of souls. Others were transmitted from Ali ibn Ahmad al-Kufi, whom the scholars of biographical evaluation described as a liar with a corrupt doctrine. Nevertheless, the large number of reports produces certainty that some of them were issued by the infallible Imams, and at the very least it produces confidence in that. Among them are reports narrated through a reliable route. So we have no need to discuss the chain of each report individually.

paragraphs.text: لأن مجموع الروايات التي نقلها المحدث النوري - ويزعم أنها اختصت بكتب الإمامية - يصل إلى 1602 رواية موزعة على النحو الآتي : * 350 رواية ( يعنى حدود ثلث الروايات التي جمعها ) من كتاب القراءات لأحمد بن محمد السياري ، وهذا الكتاب لا قيمة له عند الإمامية ومؤلفه ضعيف الحديث عند الفريقين (2) .

The total of the reports that the hadith scholar al-Nuri transmitted, which he claims are particular to the books of the Imamis, reaches 1602 reports, distributed as follows. There are 350 reports, meaning about a third of the reports he collected, from the Book of Recitations by Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari. This book has no value among the Imamis, and its author is weak in hadith according to both groups.

paragraphs.text: 874 - أحمد بن محمد بن سيار : = أحمد بن محمد البصري . = أحمد بن محمد السياري . قال النجاشي : " أحمد بن محمد بن سيار أبو عبد الله الكاتب بصري ، كان من كتاب آل طاهر ، في زمن أبي محمد ﵇ ، ويعرف بالسياري ، ضعيف الحديث ، فاسد المذهب - ذكر ذلك لنا : الحسين بن عبيد الله - مجفو الرواية ، كثير المراسيل ، له كتب ، وقع إلينا منها : كتاب ثواب القرآن ، كتاب الطب ، كتاب القراءات ، كتاب النوادر ، كتاب الغارات ، أخبرنا الحسين بن عبيد الله ، قال : حدثنا أحمد بن محمد بن يحيى ، عن أبيه ، قال : حدثني السياري ، إلا ما كان من غلو وتخليط " .

874. Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar, who is also Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Basri and Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sayyari. Al-Najashi said, "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar, Abu Abd Allah the scribe, was from Basra. He was one of the secretaries of the Al Tahir in the time of Abu Muhammad, and he is known as al-Sayyari. He is weak in hadith and corrupt in doctrine, as al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah told us. His transmission is shunned, and he has many mursal reports. He has books, of which these reached us. The Book of the Reward of the Quran, the Book of Medicine, the Book of Recitations, the Book of Rare Reports, and the Book of the Raids. Al-Husayn ibn Ubayd Allah informed us and said, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us from his father, who said, al-Sayyari narrated to me, except for what contained exaggeration (ghuluw) and confusion."

paragraphs.text: وأما الكلام في زيادته ونقصانه فمما لا يليق به أيضا ، لان الزيادة فيه مجمع على بطلانها والنقصان منه ، فالظاهر أيضا من مذهب المسلمين خلافه ، وهو الأليق بالصحيح من مذهبنا وهو الذي نصره المرتضى (ره) ، وهو الظاهر في الروايات غير أنه رويت روايات كثيره ، من جهة الخاصة والعامة ، بنقصان كثير من آي القرآن ، ونقل شئ منه من موضع إلى موضع ، طريقها الآحاد التي لا توجب علما ولا عملا ، والأولى الاعراض عنها ، وترك التشاغل بها ، لأنه يمكن تأويلها ولو صحت لما كان ذلك طعنا على ما هو موجود بين الدفتين ، فان ذلك معلوم صحته ، لا يعترضه أحد من الأمة ولا يدفعه ورواياتنا متناصرة بالحث على قراءته والتمسك بما فيه ، ورد ما يرد من اختلاف الاخبار في الفروع إليه .

The discussion of the Quran's increase and decrease is also unsuitable here. Increase in it is unanimously held to be invalid. As for decrease from it, the apparent position of the Muslims is the opposite. That is also the view more fitting for the sound position of our school, and it is the view that al-Murtada, may God have mercy on him, supported, and it is the apparent meaning of the reports.

Nevertheless, many reports have been narrated, from our own side (al-khassa) and from the general body of Muslims (al-'amma), that many verses of the Quran were diminished and that some of it was moved from one place to another. These reports come by solitary chains (ahad), which establish neither knowledge nor practice. It is better to turn away from them and to leave off occupying oneself with them, because they can be interpreted. Even if they were sound, that would not be a criticism of what exists between the two covers, because the soundness of that is known, no one in the community objects to it, and no one rejects it. Our reports agree in urging its recitation and holding fast to what is in it, and in referring back to it whatever differences arise among the reports on matters of detail.

Sa'id ibn Hibat Allah al-Rawandi, in his treatise that he wrote on the conditions of the hadiths of our companions and the proof of their soundness, from Muhammad and Ali, the two sons of Ali ibn Abd al-Samad, from their father, from Abu al-Barakat Ali ibn al-Husayn, from Abu Ja'far ibn Babawayh, from his father, from Sa'd ibn Abd Allah, from Ayyub ibn Nuh, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abd Allah, who said.

paragraphs.text: وكذا الاخبار التي تتضمن تمسك أئمة أهل البيت ﵈ بمختلف الآيات القرآنية في كل باب على ما يوافق القرآن الموجود عندنا حتى في الموارد التي فيها آحاد من الروايات بالتحريف وهذا أحسن شاهد على أن المراد في كثير من روايات التحريف من قولهم ﵈ كذا نزل هو التفسير بحسب التنزيل في مقابل البطن والتأويل . وكذا الروايات الواردة عن أمير المؤمنين وسائر الأئمة من ذريته ﵈ في إن ما بأيدي الناس قرآن نازل من عند الله سبحانه وان كان غير ما الفه علي ﵇ من المصحف ولم يشركوه ﵇ في التأليف في زمن أبى بكر ولا في زمن عثمان ومن هذا الباب قولهم ﵈ لشيعتهم : اقرؤوا كما قرء الناس ومقتضى هذه الروايات ان لو كان القرآن الدائر بين الناس مخالفا لما الفه علي ﵇ في شئ فإنما يخالفه في ترتيب السور أو في ترتيب بعض الآيات التي لا يؤثر اختلال ترتيبها في مدلولها شيئا ولا في الأوصاف التي وصف الله سبحانه بها القرآن النازل من عنده ما يختل به آثارها . فمجموع هذه الروايات على اختلاف أصنافها يدل دلالة قاطعة على أن الذي بأيدينا من القرآن هو القرآن النازل على النبي ﵌ من غير أن يفقد شيئا من أوصافه الكريمة وآثارها وبركاتها .

Likewise there are the reports that include the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt holding to various Qur'anic verses on every subject, in agreement with the Qur'an we have, even in the cases where there are isolated reports of alteration. This is the best evidence that what is meant in many of the alteration reports, in their saying "It was revealed thus," is explanation according to the revelation, as distinct from the inner meaning and the interpretation.

Likewise there are the reports from the Commander of the Faithful and the rest of the Imams from his descendants, saying that what is in the people's hands is a Qur'an sent down from God, Glorified, even though it differs from the codex that Ali compiled, and that they did not involve him in the compilation, either in the time of Abu Bakr or in the time of Uthman. To this category belongs their saying to their Shia, "Recite as the people recite." The implication of these reports is that if the Qur'an circulating among the people differs in anything from what Ali compiled, it differs only in the order of the surahs, or in the order of some verses whose disordering has no effect on their meaning. It does not differ in the attributes with which God, Glorified, described the Qur'an sent down from Him, so as to impair their effects.

So these reports taken together, despite their different kinds, indicate conclusively that the Qur'an in our hands is the Qur'an sent down upon the Prophet, without having lost any of its noble attributes, its effects, or its blessings.

O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in a state of ihram. Whoever of you kills it intentionally, the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock, as two men of justice among you judge, as an offering reaching the Kaaba; or an expiation by feeding poor people; or the equivalent of that in fasting, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. “This is one of the things in which the scribes made mistakes.” I say that his statement, and likewise the statement of al-Baqir, “This is one of the things in which the scribes made mistakes,” means that the alif in the words of the Most High, “two men of justice,” is an addition. The scribes added it by mistake, and the correct form is “a man of justice” without the alif. The “man of justice” means the Prophet, or the Imam after him.

paragraphs.text: 2 - عدة من أصحابنا ، عن أحمد بن محمد ، عن عمر بن عبد العزيز ، عن حماد بن عثمان قال : سمعت أبا عبد الله ﵇ يقول : تظهر الزنادقة في سنة ثمان وعشرين ومائة وذلك أني نظرت في مصحف فاطمة ﵍ ، قال : قلت : وما مصحف فاطمة ؟ قال : إن الله تعالى لما قبض نبيه ﵌ دخل على فاطمة ﵍ من وفاته من الحزن ما لا يعلمه إلا الله ﷿ فأرسل الله إليها ملكا يسلي غمها ويحدثها ، فشكت ذلك (1) إلى أمير المؤمنين ﵇ فقال : إذا أحسست بذلك وسمعت الصوت قولي لي فأعلمته بذلك فجعل أمير المؤمنين ﵇ يكتب كلما سمع حتى أثبت من ذلك مصحفا قال : ثم قال : أما إنه ليس فيه شئ من الحلال والحرام ولكن فيه علم ما يكون .
2. A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Hammad ibn Uthman, who said that he heard Abu Abd Allah say,
"The heretics will appear in the year one hundred and twenty-eight, and that is because I looked in the Mushaf of Fatima."
He said, "I said, 'And what is the Mushaf of Fatima?'"

He said, "When God the Exalted took back His Prophet, there came upon Fatima, because of his death, a grief that only God the Mighty and Majestic knows. So God sent her an angel to console her in her sorrow and to speak with her. She complained of this to the Commander of the Believers, and he said, 'When you sense that and hear the voice, tell me.' She told him about it, and the Commander of the Believers began to write down everything he heard, until he had put together a mushaf from it."
He said, "Then he said, 'It contains nothing of the lawful and the unlawful, but it contains knowledge of what will happen.'"
